news.title_original: Pinellas County waives residential tire disposal fee to help reduce spread of dengue fever - Pinellas County (.gov)

analysis.event: Pinellas County declared a State of Local Emergency for dengue fever and waived the residential tire disposal fee to help reduce its spread. The event is confirmed based on the official declaration.
analysis.scale_impact_and_risk: Not reported in the supplied evidence. No specific case counts, death counts, or exposure numbers are mentioned.
analysis.response_status_and_uncertainty: Pinellas County is taking measures to reduce the spread of dengue fever, including waiving the tire disposal fee. The response is under investigation as the county continues to monitor the situation.

analysis.brief_en: Pinellas County, Florida, has waived the residential tire disposal fee to help reduce the spread of dengue fever, as part of its response to a declared State of Local Emergency. The decision was made on September 28, 2026, following an emergency declaration on September 24, 2026. The county aims to minimize mosquito breeding sites by encouraging proper tire disposal, which is a known risk factor for dengue transmission. While the exact scale of the outbreak, including case counts and deaths, is not reported in the supplied evidence, the county is actively addressing the issue through public health measures. The response includes ongoing investigation and monitoring of the situation to assess its impact and manage risks effectively.

news.source_body_en: Pinellas County, Florida, has waived the residential tire disposal fee to help reduce the spread of dengue fever, as part of its response to a declared State of Local Emergency. The decision was made on September 28, 2026, following an emergency declaration on September 24, 2026. The county aims to minimize mosquito breeding sites by encouraging proper tire disposal, which is a known risk factor for dengue transmission. While the exact scale of the outbreak, including case counts and deaths, is not reported in the supplied evidence, the county is actively addressing the issue through public health measures. The response includes ongoing investigation and monitoring of the situation to assess its impact and manage risks effectively.
news.content_zh: 佛罗里达州皮尼拉斯县已免除居民轮胎处置费用,以帮助减少登革热的传播,这是其应对已宣布的本地紧急状态的一部分。该决定于2026年9月28日作出,此前于2026年9月24日发布了紧急声明。该县希望通过鼓励正确处置轮胎来减少蚊虫繁殖地,而轮胎是登革热传播的已知风险因素。尽管在提供的证据中未报告暴发的确切规模,包括病例数和死亡人数,但该县正通过公共卫生措施积极应对这一问题。应对措施包括对情况的持续调查和监测,以评估其影响并有效管理风险。

Authorities in Florida have declared states of emergency following an outbreak of dengue fever, a mosquito-borne disease that is uncommon in the U.S. Photo by Soumyabrata Roy/NurPhoto via AP by Tanner Stening September 25, 2026 Share this story Copy Link Link Copied! Email Facebook LinkedIn X (Twitter) WhatsApp Reddit Authorities in Florida have declared local states of emergency following an outbreak of dengue fever, a mosquito-borne viral disease that is uncommon in the U.S. but causes sporadic outbreaks in Florida. This month, the state recorded a rare death from the disease, which the Florida Department of Health confirmed in an email to Northeastern Global News on Friday. Its most recent data shows that there were 38 new locally acquired dengue cases between Sept. 13-19, bringing the 2026 total to 190 cases across six counties. That is on top of the 212 travel-associated cases. The virus has also been detected in 17 mosquito pools this year. Michael Johansson, a Northeastern University researcher who has studied dengue for two decades, told Northeastern Global News that the number of locally acquired cases in Florida so far this year is “clearly elevated,” particularly in the Tampa Bay area, compared to the past decade. “The number of travel-associated cases are more in the normal range,” said Johansson, a research professor of public health and health sciences. What is dengue fever? Dengue is caused by four related virus types, or different strains of the same virus: dengue virus 1, 2, 3 and 4, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, or CDC. Symptoms can range from mild to severe and commonly include fever, aches and pains, nausea, vomiting and rash, while some cases can develop into severe dengue. Symptoms usually begin within two weeks of a bite from an infected mosquito and typically last two to seven days, with most people recovering after about a week, according to the CDC. Johansson said Florida is home to both Aedes aegypti and Aedes albopictus, the two mosquito species capable of transmitting dengue. Aedes aegypti is the more common dengue vector, he said, adding that species could be associated with the local chains in the ongoing Florida outbreak. “Not all mosquitos carry dengue, but we know the right ones are there. All the ingredients are there,” Johansson said. How is it transmitted? Dengue fever is transmitted when a mosquito bites a person who has the virus in their blood, picking up the virus in the process and then passing it to someone else in the same fashion. It takes about a week for a mosquito to become a carrier, though the timing depends on the temperature. In general, the warmer the environment, the quicker the virus develops inside the mosquito, Johansson said. An “imported case” refers to someone who contracted the disease elsewhere, typically while traveling abroad, and then introduces the virus to local mosquitoes when they arrive at another location and are bitten. This could lead to more mosquitos carrying the disease, Johansson said. Johansson and his colleagues have analyzed data from Miami-Dade, where dengue transmission has been more common, and found that local spread is more likely to occur in smaller, isolated chains. He said that it is still unclear whether the rising caseload reflects one sustained chain of transmission or “multiple smaller introductions.” Editor’s Picks Inside Northeastern – NYC, a sea of color, collage and creativity In Serbia, she helped build an AI to give activists worldwide a leg up The bioinformatics escape room where guests become genetic detectives Scientists dig into the potato’s potential to fight gut inflammation Time2Learn, time to sleep: Evening practice may help language stick Global prevalence of dengue fever Dengue is most common in tropical and subtropical regions, including much of Latin America and the Caribbean, Southeast Asia and the Pacific Islands, as well as parts of Africa and the Middle East, according to the CDC. The virus is most common in regions where the Aedes mosquitoes that transmit it can survive, particularly warm climates where the mosquitoes often live in and around human communities. Dengue has expanded considerably around the world over the past several decades, according to health experts. Cases reported worldwide climbed from roughly 500,000 in 2000 to 14.6 million in 2024, though the true burden is likely much higher because many infections cause few or no symptoms and never enter official counts, according to the World Health Organization. The disease is now established as endemic in more than 100 countries, meaning that it is constantly present. “The general trends show there are more dengue cases, malaria, yellow fever and West Nile Virus reported in the U.S. over the past decade,” Richard Wamai, a Northeastern professor and an expert in neglected tropical diseases, said in an email. “And this also is the general trend globally, especially for the deadly malaria.” Wamai said the spread of dengue is exacerbated by climate change, regional gaps in disease surveillance and health education, among other factors. Warming temperatures and changing rainfall patterns, along with migration and travel, can create more favorable conditions for dengue-carrying mosquitoes to proliferate, he said. What can be done to stop the spread? Florida Surgeon General Joseph Ladapo urged residents to take protective measures, including using insect repellent, covering up when possible and removing standing water around homes. Though severe outcomes are rare, education and awareness on the part of physicians and health care providers is important because dengue is occasionally fatal, Johansson said. “Recognizing the disease and providing supportive treatment can greatly improve a patient’s chances of survival,” he said

The outbreak includes both locally acquired and travel-associated cases, with 38 new locally acquired cases reported between Sept. 13-19, bringing the 2026 total to 190 cases across six counties. Additionally, there were 212 travel-associated cases, and the virus was detected in 17 mosquito pools. A rare death from dengue was confirmed by the Florida Department of Health. Dengue is caused by four related virus types (DENV-1 to DENV-4), and the outbreak is considered elevated compared to the past decade. Researchers suggest that local spread may occur in smaller, isolated chains, and the Florida Surgeon General urged residents to take protective measures, such as using insect repellent and removing standing water, to prevent further transmission. The situation remains under investigation, with experts noting the potential for climate change and other factors to influence the spread of the virus.

news.content: English News Local Gujarat Dengue Outbreak In Gujarat: Symptoms, Prevention & Platelet Facts | 2026 Gujarat Explainer Is this the last year of dengue?: Severe fever keeps changing its form; papaya leaf remedy has no proven benefit 3 days ago Copy link Dengue cases have risen sharply across Gujarat in September, with thousands of people contracting the disease and one child reportedly dying, bringing the outbreak into greater focus. The rapid spread has raised questions about why dengue is spreading so quickly, whether a vaccine is available and whether platelet transfusions are necessary for patients. The Gujarat Explainer explores the answers to these questions. Question 1: What is the current situation regarding dengue? Answer: Dengue has worsened significantly over the past two months. Thousands of cases have been reported in September alone. The Aedes aegypti mosquitoes that transmit dengue bite only in the early morning and late evening. During the monsoon, they lay eggs in water that has accumulated everywhere, and new mosquitoes hatch from them. Then, when the sun becomes hot in Bhadarvo, the eggs laid in the water hatch because of the heat, and mosquitoes emerge and spread everywhere. This is exactly the situation now. Mosquitoes have increased after heavy monsoon rains were followed by intense heat. There are numerous dengue cases across Gujarat. In Ahmedabad, as of 27 September, around 2,000 patients are admitted to government and private hospitals. Thousands of other patients are receiving treatment at home. Patients with severe dengue have to be admitted to hospital. (Representative image) Dengue is spreading rapidly among children and the elderly. They develop a fever, body aches and severe fatigue. However, most people do not get tested. They get tested only after their condition deteriorates significantly. They put themselves at risk by taking painkillers without medical advice. Ahmedabad Municipal Corporation (AMC) recorded a total of 496 dengue cases from 1 September to 20 September, including 183 cases (about 37%) among children aged 0 to 14. An eight-year-old child living in the eastern part of the city has also died amid the rising infection. The death occurred during the first 20 days of September. Dengue cases have risen rapidly in 20 days, raising concerns that they could increase further over the next one to two months. Children, the elderly and pregnant women face a higher risk of dengue. Dengue occurs every year, but cases have risen rapidly this time. Question 2: Why have dengue cases started rising? Answer: An increase in the mosquito population is not the reason dengue has spread more. There is a shocking reason why dengue cases have increased. Explaining this, Ahmedabad senior physician Dr Tapan Shah says, "Before I explain the reason, it is important to understand some basic information about dengue. There are four types of dengue virus: DENV 1, DENV 2, DENV 3 and DENV 4. Dengue can be caused by any one of these four types of virus." For some time, DENV 1 and DENV 2 strains of the dengue virus had been spreading in Gujarat. This time, the DENV 3 strain has spread in the state. Secondly, just as the coronavirus used to change its form, any virus continues to change over time. The same is true of the dengue virus. The dengue virus has changed its form this time, which means that a medicine that worked last year may not work this year. The mutation has made the dengue virus more aggressive, and cases have increased along with it. Fever patients are literally overflowing at Civil Hospital. Dengue spreads through the Aedes aegypti mosquito. As this mosquito has black and white stripes on its body and legs, it is also known as the 'tiger mosquito'. The female mosquito lays eggs in clean, stagnant water. If a female mosquito infected with the dengue virus lays eggs, those eggs are also infected with the virus. This causes the dengue virus to spread in greater numbers. Once the dengue virus develops in a female mosquito, it remains in her throughout her life. She then spreads the virus to other people as well. The average lifespan of an Aedes aegypti mosquito is fourteen days. During its lifetime, it lays eggs three times, with approximately 100 eggs each time. Only female mosquitoes bite humans because they need human blood for the development of their eggs. They bite more frequently in the early morning and around dusk. Getting dengue means a drop in platelet count. There are many traditional remedies for it, but the most common remedy is drinking papaya leaf juice. Question 3: Can drinking papaya leaf juice cure dengue? Answer: First, understand what happens in the body when a person contracts dengue. A mosquito bites you, and its saliva enters your body. The virus present in the saliva is known as the dengue virus. The virus then mixes with the blood in your body. There are three types of cells in our blood: red blood cells (RBCs), white blood cells (WBCs) and platelets. The virus that enters our blood from the mosquito attacks the platelets first. As a result, their number in the blood begins to fall. The function of platelets is to help the blood clot. For example, if you suffer a cut or injury, the bleeding stops after a while. This happens because of the platelets. Papaya leaf juice is extracted and given to dengue patients receiving treatment at home. Suppose dengue causes platelet levels to fall, making the blood thinner. If a person with dengue suffers a wound or injury, the bleeding does not stop immediately. If a woman with dengue is menstruating, she experiences increased bleeding. This is because the platelets (thrombocytes) responsible for helping the blood clot have decreased. Have you understood this much? Now, let us talk about papaya leaves. For years, a belief has been widespread that dengue patients should be given papaya leaf juice because it increases their platelet count. Dr Tapan Shah says this is false. There is no scientific evidence that drinking papaya leaf juice increases platelet counts. Nevertheless, those who like it continue to drink it. The market is flooded with companies selling syrups made from papaya leaves. This is all a psychological effect. Whether you drink a spoonful of the juice or syrup, you feel reassured that your platelet count will now increase. But that is not what happens. Markets are flooded with piles of syrups made from papaya leaves. Pregnant women must not drink papaya leaf juice at all. It can adversely affect the baby in the womb. As for the syrups, such companies are selling various syrups in the name of papaya juice to promote their business. There is no way of knowing whether these syrups contain papaya leaves. Even if they do, they will not cure dengue. Therefore, do not trust products available in the market in the name of papaya leaves. Papaya leaves themselves should not be trusted either. Here is what Dr Shah said about the difference between belief and fact... Myth: If the platelet count falls below 20,000, platelets must be transfused from fresh blood by any means necessary. news.summary_zh: 在2026年9月,古吉拉特邦报告了一次登革热暴发,记录了数千例病例,包括一名8岁儿童的死亡。文章探讨了此次病例激增的原因,指出该病毒已发生突变,使其更具攻击性且对以往的抗病毒药物反应减弱。此次暴发引发了对该疾病传播的担忧,尤其是对儿童、老年人和孕妇群体。Aedes aegypti蚊子,俗称‘虎蚊’,是该病毒的传播媒介,其种群数量因季风降雨和随后的高温而增加。尽管木瓜叶汁常被用作疗法,但文章指出其未被证实具有疗效。目前情况仍在调查中,医院已不堪重负,许多患者在家接受治疗。文章强调应优先寻求医疗指导而非未经证实的家庭疗法,并突出了日益增长的公共卫生风险。

analysis_zh.time: 此次暴发在过去两个月内显著恶化,2026年9月病例数量急剧上升。9月前20天内一名8岁儿童死亡,且在20天内病例迅速增加,引发了对未来1至2个月内病例进一步上升的担忧。
analysis_zh.location_and_population: 此次暴发发生在古吉拉特邦,特别是在艾哈迈达巴德市,截至2026年9月27日,约有2000名患者被收治在政府和私立医院。数千名其他患者则在家接受治疗。受影响的人群包括儿童、老年人和孕妇,其中儿童0至14岁群体的病例比例显著。
analysis_zh.event: 在古吉拉特邦报告了一次登革热暴发,数千人感染了该病毒,一名儿童死亡。文章讨论了该病毒的传播、进化及其对公共卫生的影响,包括Aedes aegypti蚊子的作用以及木瓜叶汁作为疗法未被证实有效。
analysis_zh.scale_impact_and_risk: 仅在2026年9月就报告了数千例登革热病例,其中儿童病例占显著比例。一名8岁儿童的死亡引发了对该暴发严重性的担忧。文章指出该病毒已发生变化,使其更具攻击性,并增加了重症登革热的风险,尤其是在儿童、老年人和孕妇中。
analysis_zh.response_status_and_uncertainty: 此次暴发仍在调查中,报告称由于季风降雨和随后的高温,蚊子种群数量增加。文章强调了对病毒传播机制的认识重要性,并指出应优先寻求医疗建议而非未经证实的家庭疗法。应对措施包括医院收治和家庭治疗,但未提及具体的预防或控制措施。

Health Dengue fever outbreak in Florida: Symptoms, number of cases and locations where the mosquito-borne illness is spreading Greg Heilman Update: Sep 29th, 2026 10:31 EDT 0 Share facebook twitter whatsapp Make us preferred on Google Florida is experiencing what one local official called a “wildly unusual” explosion of dengue infections. So far, there have been 392 dengue fever cases reported, both linked to travel and locally acquired, according to data from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. The latter cases are of the most concern, with 190 cases of locally acquired dengue according to the most recent Florida Arbovirus Surveillance report and 17 mosquito pools in six counties. Hillsborough County is the county with the most reported cases, 177, in the Sunshine state followed by Miam-Dade County which has 132 reported cases according to the CDC. Local states of emergency have been declared in Hillsborough, home to Tampa Bay, as well as two neighboring counties, Pasco and Pinellas. This will allow them to coordinate resources more quickly to protect public health and ask for necessary funds and assistance from the state and federal government. CDC How is dengue transmitted? The Florida Department of Health says that dengue fever is “acquired through the bite of certain species of mosquitoes, primarily Aedes aegypti, but also Aedes albopictus, both of which are present in Florida.” According to the latest Florida Arbovirus Surveillance report, six counties are under mosquito-borne illness advisories including Leon, Alachua, Brevard, Walton, Palm Beach, Pasco, and Walton. The counties of Duval, Hillsborough, Maimi-Dade, Orange, and Pinellas are under mosquito-borne illnesses alerts. Here’s the Aedes aegypti risk map from @eLife the entire Gulf of Mexico is at risk (Gulf of America too) from TX to FL that could mean not only the return of dengue, but also Zika, Chikungunya, attached are my concerns about yellow fever as well, it’s why we organized a school of... https://t.co/cdtIakzay1 pic.twitter.com/hpvKiWwgee — Prof Peter Hotez MD PhD DSc(hon) (@PeterHotez) September 29, 2026 What are the symptoms of dengue, aka “breakbone fever”? People who get infected with dengue can experience a “sudden onset of fever, severe headache, eye pain, muscle and joint pain (giving the disease the nickname “breakbone fever”), and bleeding,” explains the Florida Department of Health. In some cases, those infected experience gastrointestinal symptoms like vomiting and diarrhea. In rare cases, people can contract a more severe form of the infection, dengue hemorrhagic fever, “that can be fatal if not recognized and treated with supportive care.” Symptoms appear three to fourteen days after being bitten by an infected mosquito. And they typically last for between four and seven days. “There is no treatment for dengue fever or dengue hemorrhagic fever, but quick recognition and management of symptoms and complications is effective at preventing deaths.” Related stories Get closer to the game! Where it is spreading Cheryl McCloud USA TODAY NETWORK - Florida Sept. 25, 2026, 10:22 a.m. ET Florida's dengue count is approaching the highest level seen in recent years. A major outbreak of locally acquired cases are confirmed in Hillsborough County, in the Tampa Bay area. See breakdown of dengue by county. An outbreak of dengue continues in the Tampa Bay area on Florida's west coast. Of Florida's 190 locally acquired cases of dengue as of Sept. 19, 170 have been in Hillsborough County. The remainder are scattered in five other counties in the state, mostly in South Florida, according to the Florida Department of Health. The numbers are close to the highest number in recent memory, 199 in 2023, and far higher than the 62 cases reported in all of 2025. ➤ How worried should Florida residents, visitors be about dengue? Currently, 11 counties are under either a mosquito-borne illness advisory or mosquito-borne illness alert. Shop Amazon for mosquito repellents Here's where dengue has been reported in Florida, along with symptoms to watch for. Hillsborough County leads Florida with 170 cases of dengue fever According to the Florida Department of Health, as of Sept. 19, there have been 190 cases of locally acquired cases of dengue reported in six counties, which is up from 152 reported Sept. 12. Of the 190 cases of locally acquired dengue, 170 were in Hillsborough County, according to the Florida Department of Health. ➤ Prevent dengue at home in Florida with this 10-minute mosquito inspection The county is under a mosquito-borne illness alert, according to an Aug. 12 alert update from the Hillsborough County Department of Health after the eighth case of locally acquired dengue was reported. Property owners can request a free on-site inspection from Mosquito Management Services Unit to have an inspection on their property to identify potential mosquito breeding sites. "If you feel that your neighborhood is a good candidate for mosquito spraying, you can fill out the form for a Neighborhood Spray Request. The county's mosquito spraying map shows areas sprayed within the last 28 days by both truck and aerial. 7 cases of dengue reported in Miami-Dade County As of Sept. 19, the Florida Department of Health reported there had been seven cases of locally acquired dengue confirmed in Miami-Dade County. The county issued a mosquito-borne illness alert on Aug. 3 after a confirmed case of locally acquired dengue. Miami-Dade County said residents "experiencing significant mosquito problems can submit a service request online for an inspection" or call 311. 7 cases of dengue reported in Pinellas County As of Sept. 19, the Florida Department of Health reported there had been seven cases of locally acquired dengue confirmed in Pinellas County. The county issued a mosquito-borne illness alert on Aug. 11 after two confirmed cases of locally acquired dengue. 3 cases of dengue reported in Orange County As of Sept. 19, the Florida Department of Health reported there had been three cases of locally acquired dengue confirmed in Orange County. The county issued a mosquito-borne illness advisory Sept. 2 after a confirmed case of locally acquired dengue was confirmed in the Pine Hills area and upgraded it to a mosquito-borne illness alert Sept. 18 after two additional confirmed cases of dengue were reported in the Apopka area, according to Orange County Mosquito Control. "Mosquito control crews are conducting targeted control measures and enhanced surveillance in the affected areas and across the county to reduce the risk of further local transmission in Orange County." Orange County is also under a mosquito-borne illness advisory for West Nile virus. 2 cases of dengue reported in Pasco County As of Sept. 19, the Florida Department of Health reported there had been two cases of locally acquired dengue confirmed in Pasco County. "Dengue virus has become an increasingpublic-health concern in the Greater Tampa Bay region," Pasco County Mosquito Control posted on its website. "Because our region is so interconnected, this is not simply a Hillsborough County issue or a Pasco County issue. Thousands of people travel between Pasco, Hillsborough, Pinellas, Hernando, Citrus and surrounding counties every day for work, school, healthcare, recreation and other activities. "Reducing dengue transmission wherever it is occurring in the Tampa Bay region helps reduce the opportunity for the virus to be carried into neighboring communities." 1 case of dengue reported in Palm Beach County As of Sept. 19, the Florida Department of Health reported there had been one case of locally acquired dengue confirmed in Palm Beach County. The Palm Beach County Department of Health issued a mosquito-borne illness advisory Aug. 3 after a confirmed case of locally acquired dengue fever. Residents can use an online form to report mosquito activity. Palm Beach County Mosquito Control will "verify and document the presence of a legitimate mosquito problem" before spraying. What's causing the Florida outbreak of dengue fever? "The surge in dengue cases — along with a few West Nile and the first chikungunya — in Florida is chiefly driven by a combination of climatic and human factors that create ideal conditions" for the types of mosquitoes that spread dengue, West Nile and the chikungunya viruses, said Eva Buckner, associate professor and extension specialist with the UF/IFAS Florida Medical Entomology Laboratory via email Sept. 23. The factors that creating ideal conditions for the mosquitoes responsible for transmitting the viruses include: Warmer temperatures: Summer high temperatures speed up mosquito life cycles and virus replication, allowing more mosquito generations in a single season and able to transmit viruses faster. Increased rainfall and standing water: Heavy rains and storm‐water runoff create abundant mosquito production sites in both natural and artificial containers. Outbreaks worldwide and human travel: Locations worldwide where Aedes aegypti-borne diseases like dengue and chikungunya are endemic (experience transmission every year usually year-round) are experiencing outbreaks, Buckner said. What's the difference between a mosquito-borne illness advisory and alert? "A mosquito-borne illness advisory means the public should take precautions to reduce mosquito bites due to factors indicating local disease such as positive sentinels, very few presumptive or positive human cases, or other justifications," according to Sarasota County. "A mosquito-borne illness alert means that there has been heightened disease activity, a significant increase in vector (disease capable) mosquito populations, or an increase in locally-transmitted human cases. "Residents should continue to take precautions, but exercise additional caution in preventing mosquito bites." What are symptoms of dengue, breakbone fever? "Dengue fever can be a painful, debilitating disease but is rarely fatal," the Florida Department of Health said. Symptoms appear three to 14 days after the bite of an infected mosquito and include: sudden onset of fever severe headache eye pain muscle and joint pain (giving the disease the nickname “breakbone fever”) bleeding Gastrointestinal symptoms like vomiting and diarrhea may also be present in some cases. "Dengue fever symptoms usually last four to seven days. The disease is often diagnosed incorrectly because the symptoms are similar to influenza and other viruses," the CDC said. "Around one out of every 20 people infected by a dengue virus develops severe dengue, a life-threatening medical emergency that requires immediate medical attention," according to YaleMedicine. Can dengue be treated? "While there is no cure for dengue and there are no specific medications for the condition, getting adequate hydration and plenty of rest, and taking acetaminophen for pain and fever can help alleviate symptoms while the body’s immune system fights the virus," according to YaleMedicine. "In most cases, people recover from dengue within a week. For those with severe dengue, treatment by health care professionals can significantly lower the risk of death." What are the best mosquito repellents to use? According to the Florida Department of Health, repellents with the following active ingredients provide the best protection: DEET Picaridin IR3535 Oil of lemon eucalyptus Para-menthane-diol 2-undecanone, a plant-derived ingredient Cheryl McCloud is a journalist for the USA TODAY Network-Florida's service journalism Connect team. TAK-003 reduced dengue hospitalizations, but protection varied by viral serotype. Vaccination decisions depend on local transmission, eligibility, and continued surveillance. DENGUE vaccines can reduce illness and hospitalization, but prior infection and viral serotype still shape protection. A narrative review of clinical trials, long-term follow-up, and regulatory evidence found that vaccine selection remains closely tied to baseline dengue exposure and local transmission. The question has growing relevance beyond traditionally endemic regions. The review describes expanding Aedes mosquito habitats and reports locally acquired dengue in parts of the United States. For clinicians, travel history remains important, but its absence does not rule out local exposure where transmission occurs. Why Prior Infection Matters Four distinct dengue virus serotypes complicate vaccine development. Infection with one serotype provides lasting protection against that serotype but limited protection against the others. An immune response that does not reliably neutralize a subsequent infection may contribute to antibody-dependent enhancement and more severe disease. That concern shaped use of CYD-TDV, the first authorized dengue vaccine. Its use was restricted to people with documented previous dengue infection after an increased risk of hospitalization and severe dengue emerged in some recipients who had never been infected. Baseline serostatus is therefore a clinical safety consideration, not simply a predictor of efficacy. Trial Results Reveal Uneven Protection In a Phase III trial involving more than 20,000 children and adolescents, two doses of TAK-003 were 73.3% effective against virologically confirmed dengue and 80.2% effective against dengue-related hospitalization during the first year after vaccination. At 4.5 years, the corresponding overall estimates were 61.2% and 84.1%. Protection against some serotypes remains less certain in people without prior dengue infection. A separate Brazilian Phase III trial found that one dose of Butantan-DV was 79.6% effective against symptomatic dengue over two years. Evidence was drawn mainly from periods when serotypes 1 and 2 circulated. The review also notes serious adverse event reports during its rollout; a causal relationship had not been established, and investigation was ongoing. Where Dengue Vaccination Fits The review favors population vaccination where dengue transmission and severe disease burden are sustained. In settings with sporadic transmission, it favors selective assessment based on exposure, previous infection, regulatory indications, and vaccine availability. It concludes that vaccination should accompany mosquito control, case surveillance, clinical preparedness, and continued monitoring of vaccine safety and effectiveness. Reference Esposito S and Principi N. Dengue vaccines in a changing epidemiological landscape: current evidence, unresolved challenges, and public health considerations. Vaccines. 2026;14(9):729. 29 September 2026 • In Focus Can Tarique Rahman’s plan break the Rohingya repatriation deadlock? 28 September 2026 • Geopolitical Insights DENGUE OUTBREAK DENV-3 now dominant strain Say experts; hospitals report rising admissions Updated : 4 August 2026, 08:31 • BANGLADESH SHARE Helemul Alam Helemul Alam Unable to find a seat, a woman sits on the floor with her child at Mugda Medical College Hospital in Dhaka. The child has had a fever for four days, and doctors suspect dengue while awaiting test results. According to the DGHS, at least three people died and 580 others were hospitalised with dengue in the 24 hours until 8:00am yesterday, taking this year’s death toll to 59 and total cases to 16,684. PHOTO: MEHEDI HASAN The DENV-3 serotype has become the dominant strain of the dengue virus in Bangladesh this year, replacing DENV-2, which was the most prevalent last year, according to the Institute of Epidemiology, Disease Control and Research (IEDCR). A recent IEDCR survey of 71 dengue-positive patients found that 65 (91.55 percent) were infected with DENV-3, while the remaining six (9.23 percent) had DENV-2. Tap here to add The Daily Star as a trusted source By comparison, last year’s surveillance found DENV-2 in 49.2 percent of samples, followed by DENV-3 (35.8 percent), DENV-1 (8.8 percent), and DENV-4 (6.3 percent), IEDCR Director Dr Quazi Ahmed Zaki told The Daily Star. According to dengue experts, the virus has four serotypes -- DENV-1, DENV-2, DENV-3 and DENV-4 -- each comprising several genotypes. Although DENV-2 has historically been linked to major outbreaks, disease severity depends on multiple factors rather than the serotype alone. Zaki cautioned against describing any serotype as inherently more dangerous. “It would not be scientifically accurate to label one dengue serotype as more severe on its own. Disease severity depends on factors including the viral strain, the patient’s immune response, and underlying illnesses,” he said. Zaki said the distribution of serotypes also varies across the country. “Samples from Dhaka and other urban healthcare facilities are different from those collected in the hill tracts and other rural areas,” he said. Image “The overall picture is mixed. Urban areas may show a higher concentration of one serotype, but you cannot generalise the findings for the entire country,” he said. The IEDCR director said previous dengue infection remains one of the strongest risk factors for severe disease. “People who have had dengue before face a higher risk of severe complications, including dengue shock syndrome, if they are infected again,” he said. Patients with kidney disease, liver disease, cancer, or other active infections are also at greater risk of severe illness, regardless of the infecting serotype or whether it is their first dengue infection, he added. He urged public awareness campaigns to focus on repeat infections and underlying health conditions rather than portraying one serotype as universally more dangerous. According to the Directorate General of Health Services, 59 people had died from dengue and 16,684 had been hospitalised this year as of August 3. Meanwhile, physicians say dengue admissions have increased sharply over the past two weeks. HM Nazmul Ahsan, associate professor at Shaheed Suhrawardy Medical College Hospital, said the hospital has opened two dedicated dengue wards -- one for male and the other for female patients -- after admissions rose to 15-20 patients in each admission cycle. Referring to the latest survey, he said both DENV-2 and DENV-3 are circulating this season, although DENV-3 appears to be more common. Among the four serotypes, DENV-2 and DENV-3 are more severe, Nazmul said. However, the risk of death is higher if a person who previously had dengue is infected with a different serotype, he added. He said many patients are going into shock rapidly, but clinicians have become more experienced in managing severe dengue. For all latest news, follow The Daily Star's Google News channel. “We are seeing patients who deteriorate quite quickly. However, management has improved, and most patients are receiving timely treatment,” he said. Doctors are also reporting a rise in dengue patients with hepatitis this year. “We are seeing considerably more dengue patients with hepatitis than in previous years. Some patients are also dealing with cardiac complications,” he said. He explained that dengue-associated hepatitis requires more than routine fluid management. “When dengue causes hepatitis and liver enzyme levels become markedly elevated, treatment has to be adjusted. These patients require closer monitoring and additional medications beyond standard dengue management,” he said. Ahsan urged people with persistent fever or warning signs to seek medical care promptly, saying early diagnosis and timely treatment remain the best way to prevent severe complications and deaths. supplementary_news.content_title: Florida Local Dengue Cases Reach 190 as Hillsborough Declares Emergency and September Infections Show Mosquito Spread Continuing
supplementary_news.content: Get all your news in one place. 100's of premium titles. One app. Start reading Get all your news in one place. 100's of premium titles. One news app. Start reading Medical Daily Elena Vega Sep 28, 2026, 12:40 PM Florida Local Dengue Cases Reach 190 as Hillsborough Declares Emergency and September Infections Show Mosquito Spread Continuing Florida Hillsborough CDC Hillsborough County Newsweek Pinellas the Florida Department of Health Developing Story Note: This report covers new developments in Florida's 2026 locally acquired dengue outbreak. State case figures come from the Florida Department of Health's Week 37 report, with data through Sept. 19, 2026. Hillsborough County declared a state of local emergency on Sept. 24. Numbers may change as the state releases more weekly reports and completes case investigations. Florida reported 38 new cases of locally acquired dengue in its latest weekly surveillance report, bringing the state's 2026 total to 190. The cases span six counties, and 30 of them began in September, according to the Florida Department of Health's Week 37 arbovirus report , which covers Sept. 13 to 19. Locally acquired means the person was infected by a mosquito in Florida, not while traveling. That distinction matters for anyone who gets sick without a recent trip, because neither the patient nor a clinician may think of dengue unless someone raises the possibility. Hillsborough County accounts for 170 of the 190 cases, or nearly nine in 10. The September onsets show that transmission did not stop in August, so households in affected counties still have reason to watch for fever and mention possible mosquito exposure when they seek care. Transmission Continued Into September The state counted 170 cases in Hillsborough, seven each in Miami-Dade and Pinellas, three in Orange, two in Pasco, and one in Palm Beach. By the date symptoms started, 21 cases began in July, 139 in August, and 30 so far in September. The September count is likely to rise. Symptoms start before a person is tested and the case is reported, so illnesses that began in late September may not appear until later reports. The report also counted 17 mosquito pools, or batches of trapped mosquitoes, that tested positive this year. "In 2026, 190 cases of locally acquired dengue and 17 mosquito pools have been reported from six counties," the department wrote. Dengue is caused by four related virus types. Of the 171 cases that were typed, 169 were DENV-2, and two were DENV-3. The state also reported 212 travel-associated dengue cases this year, up from 186 in the prior report, plus one locally acquired chikungunya case in Miami-Dade with onset in August. Duval, Hillsborough, Miami-Dade, Orange, and Pinellas counties are under mosquito-borne illness alerts. Illness Without Travel History Dengue spreads mainly through the bite of an infected Aedes mosquito. It does not spread through ordinary contact between people. Because dengue cases diagnosed in Florida are usually linked to travel, a fever in someone who has not left the state may not immediately suggest dengue. Kristi Miley, a researcher at the University of South Florida's Center for Global Health Infectious Disease Research, told Newsweek that "The Bay Area has seen more locally acquired cases than in previous years, indicating a localized outbreak in Hillsborough County's mosquito population rather than a statewide increase." She added that Hillsborough "has not recorded this level of dengue infection since the 1930s." "Many people may not seek care and fully recover without incidence; however it can be life-threatening for some, " Miley said. The CDC estimates that only about one in four people infected with dengue get sick, so official counts likely understate how many people have been infected. That is why telling a clinician about mosquito bites or living in an affected county matters, even without travel. Common symptoms include fever with aches and pains, such as pain behind the eyes or muscle, joint, or bone pain, along with nausea, vomiting, or rash. Symptoms typically last two to seven days, according to the CDC's dengue symptoms page . About one in 20 people who get sick develop severe dengue, a medical emergency. Warning Signs After the Fever Breaks Warning signs of severe dengue usually begin in the 24 to 48 hours after a fever goes away, when people may assume they are recovering. The CDC lists belly pain or tenderness, vomiting at least three times in 24 hours, bleeding from the nose or gums, vomiting blood or blood in the stool, and feeling extremely tired or restless as signs that require emergency care. Medication choices also matter. The CDC's dengue treatment guidance advises taking acetaminophen for fever and pain and warns, "Do not take aspirin or ibuprofen!" Those drugs can raise the risk of bleeding. According to a CDC health advisory , people at higher risk of severe dengue include infants, pregnant women, adults 65 and older, people with certain medical conditions, and people who have had a previous dengue infection and get infected again. Emergency Declaration Follows Weeks of Growth MedicalDaily previously reported that Florida's local dengue count had reached 152 , with Tampa Bay accounting for nearly all infections and 41 new cases in the prior week, the largest weekly increase this year. The newest data mark the third straight week with at least 38 new local cases, following 38 in Week 35 and 41 in Week 36. Hillsborough rose from 134 to 170 cases. Newsweek, citing the Tampa Bay Times, reported that an 80-year-old Hillsborough County woman died of dengue complications on Sept. 4, the state's first dengue death of 2026. The Florida Department of Health later confirmed the death. On Sept. 24, Hillsborough County Administrator Bonnie Wise signed an order declaring a state of local emergency over dengue . The order lasts seven days unless it is extended or rescinded, and it lets officials act quickly and seek federal reimbursement for certain costs. The county is conducting aerial mosquito treatments in several neighborhoods. Pasco and Pinellas counties declared their own local states of emergency the same week, and the Florida Department of Health in Polk County announced the county's first locally acquired case on Sept. 24. That case is not included in the Week 37 count. Practical protection has not changed. Residents should empty and scrub, turn over, cover, or throw out items that hold water, such as flowerpot saucers, buckets, pet bowls, toys, and tarps, at least once a week. They should also use EPA-registered insect repellent and keep window screens in good repair. The state releases arbovirus reports weekly, and the next update will show whether September cases keep climbing. For now, a fever after mosquito bites in an affected county is reason to call a clinician and mention dengue, whether or not the person has traveled. Key Questions Answered How many locally acquired dengue cases has Florida reported in 2026? There were 190 as of the Week 37 report, with data through Sept. 19, including 38 new cases that week. What does locally acquired mean? The person was infected by a mosquito in Florida rather than while traveling outside the state or country. Which counties have local cases? Hillsborough (170), Miami-Dade (7), Pinellas (7), Orange (3), Pasco (2), and Palm Beach (1). Is dengue still spreading? Yes. Thirty cases had September onset dates, and that number may rise as reports catch up. Polk County also announced its first local case on Sept. 24. What warning signs need emergency care? Belly pain, repeated vomiting, bleeding from the nose or gums, blood in vomit or stool, or extreme tiredness or restlessness, especially in the day or two after the fever fades. Which pain relievers should people avoid? The CDC advises acetaminophen and warns against aspirin and ibuprofen, which can increase bleeding risk. A recent death in Florida highlights the importance of recognizing symptoms and warning signs of severe dengue. The Florida Department of Health confirmed on Sept. 18, 2026, that the death of an elderly woman on Sept. 4 was due to dengue fever. It is the first confirmed dengue death in Hillsborough County, where health officials have reported multiple acquired cases. In August, the Hillsborough County Health Department issued a mosquito-borne illness alert. This cluster of locally spread cases is a stark reminder that a disease which most Americans associate with faraway tropical vacations is increasingly being caught at home. Dengue is often called “breakbone fever,” and the nickname is earned. People who get sick typically develop a sudden high fever along with a pounding headache, pain behind the eyes and deep aches in the muscles, joints and bones. Many also feel nauseated, throw up or break out in a blotchy rash a few days in. As an infectious diseases physician and tropical medicine specialist who directs a travel clinic, I see how easily dengue slips past both patients and doctors. In parts of the U.S. where the disease is still uncommon, it is easily mistaken for the flu or COVID-19, and that delay can be dangerous. How it spreads Dengue is not passed from person to person like a cold. It spreads through the bite of infected Aedes mosquitoes, mainly Aedes aegypti, a species commonly found in Florida. These mosquitoes thrive in warm cities and can breed in as little as a bottle capful of standing water. These mosquitoes bite during the day, not just at dusk. The cycle is simple and hard to break: A mosquito bites an infected person, then bites someone else days later, giving them the virus. Dengue is especially tricky because most infections cause no symptoms at all. Roughly 3 in 4 people who catch the virus never feel sick. For the 25% who are symptomatic, those symptoms don’t appear until four to 10 days after being bitten. In addition, there are four different strains of the dengue virus, and surviving one gives you lasting protection against only that one. A second infection with a different type actually raises the odds of severe disease. A life-threatening turn Most people suffer with dengue for a miserable week and then recover on their own. But about 1 in 20 patients progress to severe dengue, a life-threatening turn that tends to strike just as the fever breaks – often around days three to seven, when patients and their families may wrongly assume the worst is over. In severe dengue, tiny blood vessels throughout the body start leaking fluid, blood pressure can crash and dangerous bleeding or organ damage can follow. Warning signs that someone is sliding into this phase include severe belly pain, repeated vomiting, bleeding from the gums or nose, extreme drowsiness or restlessness, and blood in vomit or stool. Some groups face higher risk, including infants, pregnant women, adults over 65 and people with conditions like diabetes, obesity or kidney disease. Left untreated, severe dengue can kill up to 10% of patients. With prompt hospital care, that number drops below 1 in 100 – which is why recognizing it early matters so much. A dengue vaccine exists, but it is not recommended for the average American traveler. The available shots are used only in select cases, such as children who live in high-transmission areas and have already had dengue once. So prevention still rests mostly on avoiding mosquito bites. How dengue is treated There is no antiviral drug that cures dengue. Care is all about supporting the body while it fights the virus. For people well enough to stay home, that means rest, plenty of fluids and acetaminophen, commonly known in the U.S. by the brand name Tylenol, for fever and pain. Patients who may have dengue must avoid aspirin, ibuprofen and other non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs. These drugs raise the risk of bleeding, which is already a danger with dengue. Patients who develop more severe symptoms need to be admitted to the hospital, where doctors give carefully measured intravenous fluids and watch closely. Too little fluid and the patient can go into shock; too much and the lungs can flood. A worsening global problem Dengue is surging worldwide. The World Health Organization recorded more than 14 million cases in 2024, its worst year on record, across some 100 countries. That’s a 2,600% increase from the more than 505,000 cases reported in 2000. Warmer temperatures, rapid urban growth and global travel are all helping the mosquitoes – and the virus – expand into places where it has never been a problem before. South Asia, Southeast Asia and Latin America carry the heaviest burden, but the map is spreading north. Why the U.S. should pay attention Most U.S. dengue cases are still picked up abroad. Travelers return home sick. In 2023 alone, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention reported nearly 1,900 such travel-related cases. But every infected traveler is a spark, and in warm states the tinder is already there. In the U.S. territories, Puerto Rico and the U.S. Virgin Islands see the most cases by far. Florida has the highest risk among the 50 states, with Miami-Dade County recording more than 300 locally acquired dengue infections between 2010 and 2024. Local cases have also turned up in Texas, California, Arizona and Hawaii. What to do if you think you have dengue If you develop a sudden fever after traveling to a dengue-prone area, or after mosquito exposure in South Florida, see a doctor and mention where you’ve been. Rest, drink fluids and use acetaminophen – not ibuprofen or aspirin. Most importantly, watch for the warning signs. Severe belly pain, repeated vomiting, bleeding or sudden drowsiness means get to an emergency room right away. And to protect yourself and your neighbors: Use insect repellent, wear long sleeves and dump out any standing water in your yard where mosquitoes breed. This article originally appeared in The Conversation. Key Points Dengue is increasingly being transmitted locally in the U.S. Most infections cause no symptoms, while some can progress to severe disease. Severe dengue can emerge as a fever begins to subside. Florida currently faces the greatest risk among the 50 states. Why did Florida counties declare dengue emergencies? topics: Dengue Florida Local emergency Mosquito control Aedes aegypti Aedes albopictus Hillsborough Pasco WEST PALM BEACH, Fla. (CBS12) — Dengue fever is spreading in Florida, prompting three counties to declare local states of emergency over the mosquito-borne disease. Pasco County declared a local state of emergency Sept. 23. Hillsborough and Pinellas counties followed the next day. The declarations allow local officials to bolster mosquito-control efforts and access emergency resources. Each declaration must be renewed to remain in effect beyond seven days. The latest Florida Department of Health surveillance report shows 190 locally acquired dengue cases statewide this year across six counties. Hillsborough County accounts for 170 cases, followed by Miami-Dade and Pinellas with seven each, Orange with three, Pasco with two and Palm Beach County with one. The report covers cases with onset through Sept. 19. Dengue is spread by Aedes aegypti and Aedes albopictus mosquitoes. It can cause flu-like symptoms, including aches and pains, nausea, vomiting and rash. In severe cases, it can lead to internal bleeding, shock and death. Florida is experiencing one of its most significant dengue fever outbreaks in years, with case numbers rising statewide and the state's first virus-related death confirmed by the Florida Department of Health in early September. "It's one of the worst years for dengue that Florida has had in some time," said Tulane University medical entomologist Dawn Wesson. "They'll have a few locally transmitted cases most years, but not this many. It's also a little unique in that it's further north than where most previous outbreaks have hit, which tend to be closer to the Miami-Dade area." Wesson, who directs Tulane's Vector-Borne Infectious Disease Initiative and has studied dengue and other vector-borne viruses for more than three decades, said the outbreak is being driven by a combination of climate and human travel that allow Aedes mosquitoes to thrive and spread the virus. "Part of it is climate," said Wesson, associate professor of tropical medicine at Tulane’s Celia Scott Weatherhead School of Public Health and Tropical Medicine. "But it's also that people travel all over the world, and people coming into airports like Miami disperse into the surrounding area, and some of them are infected with dengue. They bring the virus in and set off local transmission.” Two Aedes species spread dengue: Aedes aegypti, the primary vector, which originated in Africa, and Aedes albopictus, the Tiger mosquito, native to Southeast Asia, which is believed to have arrived in the U.S. in the mid-1980s in shipments of used scrap tires. Unlike many mosquitoes found in the U.S., Aedes bite during the day and are recognizable by their black-and-white banded markings. They lay their eggs in natural containers like tree holes as well as man-made ones such as tires. “Tires tend to be a real problem for all these container-inhabiting mosquitoes,” Wesson added. Wesson said the mosquitoes are especially difficult to control and current tools remain limited. Medical entomologists like Wesson are pursuing ways to kill them outright or alter them genetically or bacterially so they can't transmit the virus as well. "That's the kind of stuff that keeps me up at night and keeps me busy," Wesson said. Wesson has traveled the world researching new tools to fight dengue, including projects in South America, and has served in advisory roles with local parish and regional mosquito control boards. For everyday protection from mosquitoes, Wesson recommends DEET-based repellent as well as long sleeves and a hat. Dengue outbreaks are also surging elsewhere in the world, including a major outbreak currently ongoing in Bangladesh. In the U.S., locally acquired dengue cases have also been reported in Hawaii, Texas, California and Arizona in past years. To schedule an interview, please contact Addison DeHaven, assistant director of media relations at Tulane University, at [email protected] or 605-651-2567. supplementary_news.content: Search news Forecasts Radar News More Sign in Get PremiumUpgrade Advertisement Dengue surge becomes Florida's largest outbreak on record A local outbreak of the mosquito-borne virus has spread across Central Florida. ByJonathan Belles• 7 hours ago Updated: September 30, 2026, 12:33 pm EDTPublished: September 30, 2026, 6:30 am EDT View comments Share A female Aedes aegypti mosquito in the process of acquiring a blood meal from a human host. (James Gathany/Centers for Disease Control and Prevention via AP) BETA DeeperDive is a GenAI Answer Engine built for trusted publishers. It delivers clear answers and real-time content based on what people are reading now — showcasing various stories from the The Weather Channel Network that highlight not just what happened, but why it matters. This is currently a BETA being quality assessed by human beings. Mistakes may occur. Please reference surfaced articles to validate AI summary Explore DeeperDive Ask The Weather Channel anything Who was the first dengue death in Tampa Bay this year? How many dengue cases surpassed Florida's 2023 record? Why is warming climate linked to dengue spread in Florida? Florida is in the midst of its largest dengue fever outbreak on record with more than 190 cases this year, including at least 38 new cases in September. Dengue is a tropical viral infection caused by a virus transmitted to humans by infected mosquitoes. It is most common in tropical and subtropical climates, especially in urban and suburban communities. An 80-year-old Hillsborough County woman died at Tampa General Hospital at the beginning of the outbreak as a result of a mosquito bite she received near Tampa Bay. Weather in your inbox Forecast Location Sign Up By signing up you agree to the Terms & Privacy Policy. Unsubscribe at any time. Kristi Miley, who teaches at USF's College of Public Health, told the Tampa Bay Times that this is the first reported death from a dengue infection this year and the first in Tampa Bay in almost a century. Hillsborough County leads the number of cases in the state with 170, followed by seven each in Miami-Dade and Pinellas counties. Orange County recorded three cases, Pasco reported two and Palm Beach County reported a single case, through Sept. 19. Orange County, where Orlando is located, issued its first mosquito-borne illness alert earlier this month for the first time since 2011's West Nile virus outbreak. Neighboring Polk County followed shortly after. Get More of Our News on Google Set The Weather Company as a 'Preferred Source' to get quicker access to the news you value. Pasco, Hillsborough and Pinellas counties, located in Tampa Bay, have each declared local states of emergency to speed up their response. Workers near Tampa have been spraying to kill mosquitoes day and night. They also have been checking properties for pooled water, including in tires, where mosquitoes might breed, said Paolo Pecora, senior environmental scientist for Hillsborough County Mosquito Management Services. Dengue is not native to Florida, but the state's warm, humid climate makes it an ideal setting for mosquitoes to breed. Florida is not unfamiliar with other mosquito-borne diseases, including West Nile. Mosquito activity typically peaks in the rainy season between June and September, but can remain high into the fall as standing water for mosquito breeding grounds slowly dries up. Mosquitoes can remain active year-round, especially in southern Florida. The planet's warming temperatures are likely to expand both the geographical range and the active season of mosquitoes. Key takeaways: Locally acquired cases of the mosquito-borne illness have shifted from its traditional footprint of South Florida. “I am really concerned about this,” an expert said. Three Florida counties have declared states of emergency due to a surge in locally acquired dengue fever, a mosquito-borne illness that has circulated in Florida for years. But unlike previous dengue outbreaks in the state, which were mostly centered in South Florida, the numbers show a new trend for 2026: The viral illness is moving north, specifically to the state’s central Gulf Coast. The Florida Department of Health has confirmed a total of 190 locally acquired cases of dengue, a mosquito-borne illness, in 2026. Source: James Gathany/CDC “What’s happening here is something different,” Nicole Iovine , MD, PhD, chief hospital epidemiologist at UF Health Shands Hospital in Gainesville, Florida, told Healio. “We always see some local acquisition of dengue — typically in South Florida. What's so notable now is that it made a jump north to the Tampa area.” The Florida Department of Health has confirmed a total of 190 locally acquired dengue cases as of Sept. 19 — 170 of those in Hillsborough County, which encompasses Tampa. Hillsborough, Pasco and Pinellas counties declared local states of emergency this month in response to the dengue surge. Last year, Hillsborough reported just one such case. Florida has also recorded 212 travel-associated dengue cases in 2026. But it is the amount of locally acquired dengue cases in the state that has exploded, already tripling last year’s count of 62, and surpassing Florida's recent peak of 176 set in 2023. “I am really concerned about this,” Iovine said. Moreover, this year’s El Niño weather pattern should extend warm, wet weather through the winter and keep dengue-carrying mosquitoes alive, Iovine said. “That’s just going to increase the threat because mosquitoes will be around for the winter potentially, as opposed to being killed off by a few days of a cold, hard freeze, like we normally hope for,” she said. Dengue is known as “break-bone fever” because of the crushing aches and pains it can cause for some people in the joints, legs and back, the CDC notes. “It feels like your bones are breaking, which is hard to imagine what that must feel like,” Iovine said. “These patients feel miserable.” Other symptoms include fever, nausea, vomiting and a rash, according to the CDC. Severe cases occur in around 5% of people and can be life-threatening within a few hours, the agency notes. Florida health officials have reported one dengue-related death this year — an 80-year-old Tampa woman who died on Sept. 4, according to the Tampa Bay Times . Dengue virus is transmitted to people via the bite of an infected Aedes species mosquito, primarily Aedes aegypti , according to the CDC. It is common in tropical and subtropical areas worldwide. WHO estimates that around half the world’s population is at risk for dengue. The surge in Florida comes on the heels of the discontinuation of the only dengue vaccine ever licensed for use in the U.S. The FDA approved the vaccine, Dengvaxia, in 2019 for children aged 9 to 16 years living in U.S. territories where dengue is endemic, including American Samoa, Guam, Puerto Rico and the U.S. Virgin Islands. But the vaccine, which is complicated to administer and available only to children with a confirmed previous dengue infection, was pulled from the market by Sanofi Pasteur because of a lack of demand. “The good news is we know how to make a vaccine — that's kind of the first big step that's already been done,” Iovine said. “It'll be very interesting to watch in the pharmaceutical space to see whether or not any decisions will now be made to bring (the vaccine) back to market.” Another dengue vaccine manufactured by Takeda is available in other countries outside the U.S. Takeda voluntarily pulled its FDA application for the vaccine in 2023 after the agency cited a lack of data that it protects against all four dengue serotypes. Miami-Dade County said residents "experiencing significant mosquito problems can submit a service request online for an inspection" or call 311. 7 cases of dengue reported in Pinellas County As of Sept. 19, the Florida Department of Health reported there had been seven cases of locally acquired dengue confirmed in Pinellas County. The county issued a mosquito-borne illness alert on Aug. 11 after two confirmed cases of locally acquired dengue. 3 cases of dengue reported in Orange County As of Sept. 19, the Florida Department of Health reported there had been three cases of locally acquired dengue confirmed in Orange County. The county issued a mosquito-borne illness advisory Sept. 2 after a confirmed case of locally acquired dengue was confirmed in the Pine Hills area and upgraded it to a mosquito-borne illness alert Sept. 18 after two additional confirmed cases of dengue were reported in the Apopka area, according to Orange County Mosquito Control. "Mosquito control crews are conducting targeted control measures and enhanced surveillance in the affected areas and across the county to reduce the risk of further local transmission in Orange County." Orange County is also under a mosquito-borne illness advisory for West Nile virus. 2 cases of dengue reported in Pasco County As of Sept. 19, the Florida Department of Health reported there had been two cases of locally acquired dengue confirmed in Pasco County. "Dengue virus has become an increasingpublic-health concern in the Greater Tampa Bay region," Pasco County Mosquito Control posted on its website. "Because our region is so interconnected, this is not simply a Hillsborough County issue or a Pasco County issue. Thousands of people travel between Pasco, Hillsborough, Pinellas, Hernando, Citrus and surrounding counties every day for work, school, healthcare, recreation and other activities. "Reducing dengue transmission wherever it is occurring in the Tampa Bay region helps reduce the opportunity for the virus to be carried into neighboring communities." 1 case of dengue reported in Palm Beach County As of Sept. 19, the Florida Department of Health reported there had been one case of locally acquired dengue confirmed in Palm Beach County. The Palm Beach County Department of Health issued a mosquito-borne illness advisory Aug. 3 after a confirmed case of locally acquired dengue fever. Residents can use an online form to report mosquito activity. Palm Beach County Mosquito Control will "verify and document the presence of a legitimate mosquito problem" before spraying. What's causing the Florida outbreak of dengue fever? "The surge in dengue cases — along with a few West Nile and the first chikungunya — in Florida is chiefly driven by a combination of climatic and human factors that create ideal conditions" for the types of mosquitoes that spread dengue, West Nile and the chikungunya viruses, said Eva Buckner, associate professor and extension specialist with the UF/IFAS Florida Medical Entomology Laboratory via email Sept. 23. The factors that creating ideal conditions for the mosquitoes responsible for transmitting the viruses include: Warmer temperatures: Summer high temperatures speed up mosquito life cycles and virus replication, allowing more mosquito generations in a single season and able to transmit viruses faster. Increased rainfall and standing water: Heavy rains and storm‐water runoff create abundant mosquito production sites in both natural and artificial containers. Outbreaks worldwide and human travel: Locations worldwide where Aedes aegypti-borne diseases like dengue and chikungunya are endemic (experience transmission every year usually year-round) are experiencing outbreaks, Buckner said. What's the difference between a mosquito-borne illness advisory and alert? "A mosquito-borne illness advisory means the public should take precautions to reduce mosquito bites due to factors indicating local disease such as positive sentinels, very few presumptive or positive human cases, or other justifications," according to Sarasota County. "A mosquito-borne illness alert means that there has been heightened disease activity, a significant increase in vector (disease capable) mosquito populations, or an increase in locally-transmitted human cases. "Residents should continue to take precautions, but exercise additional caution in preventing mosquito bites." What are symptoms of dengue, breakbone fever? "Dengue fever can be a painful, debilitating disease but is rarely fatal," the Florida Department of Health said. Symptoms appear three to 14 days after the bite of an infected mosquito and include: sudden onset of fever severe headache eye pain muscle and joint pain (giving the disease the nickname “breakbone fever”) bleeding Gastrointestinal symptoms like vomiting and diarrhea may also be present in some cases. "Dengue fever symptoms usually last four to seven days. The disease is often diagnosed incorrectly because the symptoms are similar to influenza and other viruses," the CDC said. "Around one out of every 20 people infected by a dengue virus develops severe dengue, a life-threatening medical emergency that requires immediate medical attention," according to YaleMedicine. Can dengue be treated? "While there is no cure for dengue and there are no specific medications for the condition, getting adequate hydration and plenty of rest, and taking acetaminophen for pain and fever can help alleviate symptoms while the body’s immune system fights the virus," according to YaleMedicine. "In most cases, people recover from dengue within a week. For those with severe dengue, treatment by health care professionals can significantly lower the risk of death." What are the best mosquito repellents to use? According to the Florida Department of Health, repellents with the following active ingredients provide the best protection: DEET Picaridin IR3535 Oil of lemon eucalyptus Para-menthane-diol 2-undecanone, a plant-derived ingredient Cheryl McCloud is a journalist for the USA TODAY Network-Florida's service journalism Connect team. There are steps you can take to reduce areas where mosquitoes can breed around your home. Take 10 minutes to walk around your home. Here's what to look for. There have been 190 locally acquired cases of dengue fever in Florida, as of the latest report from the Florida Department of Health. Also reported in the state this year are a few cases of West Nile virus and chikungunya. ➤ How worried should Florida residents, visitors be about dengue? What they all have in common is they are all transmitted by mosquitoes, and people who have gotten sick were bitten by mosquitoes here in Florida. With mosquitoes so common in Florida, is there anything you can you do help prevent being bitten by a mosquito around your home? Shop Amazon for mosquito repellents The answer is yes, and here are suggestions from experts you can follow to make a 10-minute inspection around your home to mosquito-proof your property today. ➤ Meet the mosquito, the world's deadliest animal Dengue fever spreading in Florida. See counties reporting mosquito-borne illnesses According to the Florida Department of Health, as of Sept. 19, there have been 190 cases of locally acquired cases of dengue reported in six counties, which is up from 152 reported Sept. 12 . There also have been five cases of West Nile virus and one case of chikungunya. Dengue: 190 cases 170 in Hillsborough County 7 in Miami-Dade County 7 in Pinellas County 2 in Pasco County 3 in Orange County 1 in Palm Beach County West Nile: 5 1 in Alachua County 2 in Duval County (1 an asymptomatic blood donor) 1 in Leon (asymptomatic blood donor) 1 in Walton County Chikungunya: 1 1 in Miami-Dade County What's causing the Florida outbreak of dengue fever? "The surge in dengue cases — along with a few West Nile and the first chikungunya — in Florida is chiefly driven by a combination of climatic and human factors that create ideal conditions" for the types of mosquitoes that spread dengue, West Nile and the chikungunya viruses, said Eva Buckner, associate professor and extension specialist with the UF/IFAS Florida Medical Entomology Laboratory via email Sept. 23. Increased rainfall and standing water: Heavy rains and storm‐water runoff create abundant mosquito production sites in both natural and artificial containers. Outbreaks worldwide and human travel: Locations worldwide where Aedes aegypti-borne diseases like dengue and chikungunya are endemic (experience transmission every year usually year-round) are experiencing outbreaks, Buckner said. 10-minute inspection around your home to prevent mosquito bites, spread of disease "Everyone statewide, regardless of if they are in the area of a dengue outbreak or not, should practice mosquito bite prevention," Buckner said. "It’s also important to eliminate standing water around your home once a week. Aedes aegypti and Culex mosquitoes can develop in very small amounts of water." Walk around your home and follow these steps suggested by the Florida Department of Health and CDC: Drain any standing irrigation or rain water that has collected in garbage cans, house gutters, pool covers, coolers, toys, flower pots or other containers, old tires, pool covers. Protect boats and vehicles from rain with tarps that don’t accumulate water. Maintain swimming pools in good condition and ensure they are appropriately chlorinated. Empty plastic swimming pools when not in use. Discard old items that aren’t being used and are storing water. Empty and clean birdbaths and pet water bowls once or twice weekly. Check around faucets and air conditioner units, and repair leaks or puddles that remain for several days. Remove, drain or fill tree holes and stumps with mortar; Irrigate lawns and gardens carefully to prevent water from standing for several days. Cut down weeds adjacent to home and in yards, and mow the lawn regularly. If bromeliads are part of your landscaping, flush the water out of them at least once a week. You also can coat the water in the bromeliads with a small amount of food-grade oil. Or treat the water in your bromeliads with a safe larvicide containing Bacillus thuringiensis israelensis. You can also use the larvicide in birdbaths, rain barrels, decorative fountains, and ponds. Use larvicides to treat large bodies of water that will not be used for drinking and cannot be covered or dumped out. Use an outdoor adulticide to kill adult mosquitoes in areas where they rest. Mosquito-borne illness alerts, advisories issued for these Florida counties A mosquito-borne illness advisory has been issued for the following counties: Alachua Brevard Leon Palm Beach Pasco Walton A mosquito-borne illness alert has been issued for the following counties: Duval Hillsborough Miami-Dade Orange Pinellas "A mosquito-borne illness advisory means the public should take precautions to reduce mosquito bites due to factors indicating local disease such as positive sentinels, very few presumptive or positive human cases, or other justifications," according to Sarasota County. Can dengue fever be treated? "In most cases, people recover from dengue within a week. For those with severe dengue, treatment by health care professionals can significantly lower the risk of death." outbreak claims six more lives, death toll rises to 239 Bangladesh Battles Severe Dengue Outbreak, Fatalities Reach 239 in 2023 T The Hawk· 🏷 Sep 29, 2026, 09:15 PM(Updated Oct 01, 2026, 02:06 AM) Discover more Online news portal Digital news access Epaper access pass Dhaka, Sep 29 (IANS) As many as six people died due to dengue in Bangladesh in the 24 hours until 8 am (local time) on Tuesday, raising the fatalities from the mosquito-borne disease in 2026 to 239, local media reported. During the same period, 1,942 new dengue patients were admitted to hospitals in Bangladesh, according to the Directorate General of Health Services (DGHS). Among the total deaths, 52.9 per cent were women and 47.1 per cent men, United News of Bangladesh (UNB) reported. News subscription service As many as 77,672 dengue patients have been hospitalised in Bangladesh since January 1. Among them, 72,008 people have recovered from the mosquito-borne disease. As Bangladesh grapples with a worsening dengue outbreak, country's Prime Minister Tarique Rehman on September 6 ordered the authorities to increase cleanliness drives and public awareness campaigns to prevent the spread of dengue, UNB reported. Dengue is a viral infection caused by the dengue virus (DENV), which is transmitted to humans through the bite of infected mosquitoes. There is no specific treatment for dengue and early detection and access to proper medical care lowers fatality rates of severe dengue. Bangladesh has reported a sharp increase in dengue deaths and cases in recent years compared with the 18 years from 2000-2018, local media reported. Bangladesh reported 296 dengue deaths and 50,208 cases from 2000 to 2018. In the following seven years and nine months, the fatalities from the mosquito-borne disease rose to 3,466 deaths and 7,86,091 cases, Bangladesh-based The Daily Star reported. The dengue deaths in Bangladesh were about 11.71 times the earlier figure, while reported cases were about 15.66 times higher. Public health expert Mushtuq Husain said that long-term, coordinated and people-centred public health programme was required for sustainable dengue control. Husain said Aedes mosquitoes had adapted to different environments and could breed even in small amounts of stagnant water and their spread was no longer confined to urban regions, The Daily Star reported. Husain stated that the increase in population and repeated infections were further complicating the situation. He further said that people who were previously infected with dengue could again contract the disease, while communities with little or no previous exposure are also reporting dengue infections. --IANS akl/as Continue reading BangladeshDenguePublic healthMosquito-borne diseaseOutbreakInfectious Disease About UsPrivacy PolicyContact UsEpaperNewslettersSitemap Powered by ZedBlu Tech Pvt.
