supplementary_news.content: Epaper Daily Thanthi Thanthi TV Add as Preferred on Epaper Daily Thanthi Thanthi TV Chennai Tamil Nadu India World Entertainment Entertainment Cinema OTT Business Sports Lifestyle Technology Videos Explainers Editor's Picks Tamil Nadu Dengue & monsoon fevers in Tamil Nadu: Symptoms, testing, platelet count, warning signs & prevention Here are some key questions to help readers understand when to seek testing and medical attention. Amid a rise in dengue cases, the Tamil Nadu Health and Family Welfare Department has intensified surveillance across the StateJUSTIN Online Desk Updated on: 30 Sep 2026, 6:28 am Add DT Next as your Preferred Source.See our stories first in Google Search & Top Stories Add as Preferred Source Copied Follow Us Quick summary Through official health channels: Consult a doctor if you develop persistent fever or dengue-like symptoms → get the recommended dengue test based on the illness stage → monitor platelet counts and other blood parameters as advised → seek urgent care if warning signs such as severe abdominal pain, repeated vomiting or bleeding appear → prevent dengue by eliminating stagnant water and report mosquito-related concerns through the GCC’s 1913 helpline. CHENNAI: As monsoon-related illnesses increase, fever can often be difficult to identify by symptoms alone. Dengue, seasonal viral infections and other mosquito-borne diseases may initially appear similar. Here are some key questions to help readers understand when to seek testing and medical attention. ALSO READ Granite baron Veeramani booked under POSCO Act in suicide case What are the common symptoms of dengue? Dengue commonly begins with a sudden high fever. Other symptoms can include severe headache, pain behind the eyes, muscle and joint pain, nausea, vomiting and skin rashes. However, these symptoms can overlap with other viral infections. A doctor may recommend a blood test to confirm dengue rather than relying on symptoms alone. How can dengue be different from a regular seasonal viral fever? There is no reliable way to distinguish dengue from every other viral fever based only on symptoms. Dengue may be suspected when high fever is accompanied by intense body or joint pain, headache, pain behind the eyes, nausea or rash. Persistent or worsening symptoms should be medically evaluated, particularly during periods when dengue cases are circulating. Fever cases rise in Chennai, dengue surveillance intensified When should someone get tested for dengue? The appropriate test can depend on how many days the person has had symptoms. Tests that detect the dengue virus or its NS1 antigen are generally useful during the early stage of illness, while antibody testing becomes more useful later. A doctor can determine which test is appropriate based on the patient's symptoms and the stage of the illness. Where can people get free fever testing at government facilities in Chennai? Government healthcare facilities in Chennai provide services for people presenting with fever, including evaluation for dengue and other infections. The Greater Chennai Corporation's health facilities include Urban Primary Health Centres and diagnostic centres offering investigations. People should check with the particular government facility for its current testing availability and timings before visiting. Rising dengue cases put Tamil Nadu hospitals on alert Are dengue tests available free of cost at government centres? Diagnostic investigations are available free of cost at several Greater Chennai Corporation facilities. Availability can vary depending on the centre and the test required, so patients should confirm the service at the facility. What platelet count is considered dangerous in dengue? Platelet numbers are only one part of assessing a dengue patient's condition. A falling platelet count does not automatically mean that a platelet transfusion is required. A count below 10,000 platelets per microlitre is generally considered a level at which prophylactic platelet transfusion may be considered in dengue patients who do not have bleeding, according to India's national dengue management guidance. Active bleeding and the patient's overall clinical condition are also important factors. Patients should not attempt to interpret platelet reports on their own. Doctors may monitor platelet counts along with other blood parameters and signs of bleeding or plasma leakage. Dengue, fever cases on the rise in Chennai; Adyar, Anna Nagar, Valasaravakkam turn hotspots Does every dengue patient with low platelets need a platelet transfusion? No. A low platelet count by itself does not necessarily mean a transfusion is required. Clinical condition, bleeding and other complications are considered when deciding treatment. This is particularly important because platelet counts can fall during dengue and then recover as the patient improves. What are the warning signs that require urgent medical attention? Immediate medical assessment is important if a person with suspected or confirmed dengue develops symptoms such as severe abdominal pain, repeated vomiting, bleeding from the nose or gums, blood in vomit or stools, unusual drowsiness, extreme weakness or restlessness. The period around the time the fever comes down can also be critical, so improvement in temperature does not always mean the illness has passed. How can residents help prevent dengue in their neighbourhood? The dengue mosquito breeds in stagnant water. Residents should regularly empty or cover containers that can collect water, including buckets, pots, discarded tyres and other outdoor items. Keeping surroundings free of water accumulation can reduce mosquito breeding and help protect the wider community. Where can Chennai residents report stagnant water or mosquito-related concerns? Residents can report public-health and mosquito-related complaints to the Greater Chennai Corporation (GCC) through its civic grievance channels, including the 1913 helpline. Providing the exact location of stagnant water can help civic teams identify and address potential mosquito-breeding sites. What should someone do if they develop a fever during the monsoon? Do not assume that every monsoon fever is dengue or, conversely, that dengue can be ruled out because symptoms appear mild. People with persistent fever or symptoms suggestive of dengue should consult a healthcare professional and follow the recommended testing and monitoring schedule. Self-medication, particularly with medicines that can increase bleeding risk, should be avoided unless advised by a doctor. supplementary_news.content: Skip to main content E-PAPER ARCHIVE Today's FE AUTO বাংলা Wednesday • 30 September 2026 Home Economy▾ Stock▾ Trade National▾ World▾ Editorial Views▾ More categories▾ Our Correspondent Published: Sep 27, 2026, 05:35 Share this news Country | 3 days ago Dengue outbreak takes a lethal turn in Rajshahi Dengue patients receiving treatment inside mosquito nets at Rajshahi Medical College Hospital (RMCH) in Rajshahi city amid a recent surge in infection of the deadly disease in the region. — FE Photo Infectious Diseases Our Correspondent Published: Sep 27, 2026, 05:35 RAJSHAHI, Sept 26: Dengue epidemic becomes critical in the Rajshahi region as patients are pouring into Rajshahi Medical College Hospital (RMCH) with severe complications, including dengue shock syndrome (DSS) and myocarditis. More than 25 new dengue patients are being admitted to the hospital on average every day. In several recent cases, patients' condition deteriorated rapidly and they died within hours of admission. According to RMCH data, dengue admissions began on June 7 this year, while deaths were first reported in August. As of Friday, 13 dengue patients died at the hospital, while a total of 901 patients had been admitted. Of the admitted patients, 833 were adults, including 610 men and 223 women, while 68 were children. A total of 802 patients have so far been discharged after treatment. The recent trend is particularly alarming. Eleven dengue patients died at RMCH between August 31 and September 25. Ten of them died from dengue shock syndrome, while one died from a dengue-related cardiac complication. The cases show how quickly severe dengue can turn fatal. On September 9, Pabna's Bera resident Imrul Kayes died just one and a half hours after being admitted to the hospital with dengue. The following day, college student Jeet Sarker of Bonpara in Natore died around 15 hours after admission. City & Local Guides Hridoy, a resident of Bholahat in Chapainawabganj, died on September 14 after being admitted the previous morning. The next day, housewife Asma Khatun of Balubagan in Chapainawabganj died after being admitted the previous evening. Tanore resident Anwar Mondal died about eight hours after admission on September 18. School student Sathi Rani of Bagmara, who was admitted on September 19, died early the following morning. Abdul Karim of Battala Hat in Chapainawabganj died on September 21 after five days of treatment. Nasrin, a working woman from Sultannabad in Rajshahi city, died on September 24, four days after being admitted. Doctors say dengue shock syndrome is one of the most serious complications of dengue. Excessive plasma leakage from blood vessels reduces the effective volume of circulating blood, causing a sharp fall in blood pressure and impairing blood flow to vital organs. Without timely treatment, the patient's condition can deteriorate rapidly. Myocarditis, or inflammation of the heart muscle, is another complication drawing concern among doctors. It can affect the heart's normal function and may cause a rapid deterioration in the patient's condition. Doctors at RMCH say delayed hospitalisation is one of the major concerns behind the recent deaths. Many patients initially treat fever at home or seek local treatment, assuming it to be a common viral infection. They often reach the hospital only after serious complications have developed. Medical Facilities & Services RMCH spokesperson Dr Sheikh Shamim Ahmed said many patients were arriving at the hospital at a very advanced stage because they were ignoring fever or spending valuable time on local treatment. "When patients develop complications such as dengue shock syndrome or myocarditis, it becomes difficult to save them even with treatment," he said. He advised people to consult a doctor as soon as fever develops and undergo an NS1 test when recommended. He also urged patients to seek immediate medical attention if they experience severe weakness, abdominal pain, vomiting, bleeding, breathing difficulties, unusual drowsiness or reduced urine output. Meanwhile, the Rajshahi City Corporation (RCC) says it has intensified its mosquito-control activities across the city. Cleaning drives, destruction of potential Aedes breeding sites and mosquito-control operations are being conducted in different wards. RCC chief cleanliness officer Sheikh MdMamun Dollar said the corporation's anti-dengue campaign was continuing across all wards, with greater emphasis on eliminating Aedes breeding sites. Rajshahi district entomologist Umme Habiba said Aedes larvae and adult mosquitoes were being found in common household containers and other small water-holding places. Hospitals & Treatment Centers Deputy Commissioner Kazi Shahidul Islam stressed prevention and community participation in containing the outbreak. "Stagnant water and an unclean environment create ideal conditions for Aedes breeding. Prevention must come before treatment. We need to remove stagnant water and destroy potential breeding sites around homes and other premises," he said. "As part of the three-month nationwide dengue prevention and cleanliness campaign, cleanliness drives are being conducted simultaneously every Saturday at 78 locations across nine upazilas of the district," he said. anaetru@gmail.com Our Correspondent Published: Sep 27, 2026, 05:35 Share this news Our Correspondent Published: Sep 29, 2026, 04:03 Share this news Country | 1 day ago Tk 7.48b project, taken after 'worst' floods, delayed for a year in Sylhet A view of CC blocks for the FREAP project in Sylhet. — FE photo Health Conditions Our Correspondent Published: Sep 29, 2026, 04:03 SYLHET, Sept 28: Implementation of a Tk 7.48 billion project to protect about 80,000 hectares of farmland from early floods and restoration of infrastructure to facilitate water recession on those lands located in Sylhet's three divisions was delayed with the deadline extended a year till June 2027. The project was taken after devastating floods in these regions in 2022. Some of the project's schemes, which include restoring 103.73 km of flood control embankment and construction of 15 flood fuses, have not seen almost any development for more than the last two months. Improvement of submersible embankment by armouring through cement concrete (CC) blocks and five km river protection works are also part of the project titled 'Flood Reconstruction Emergency Assistance Project' (FREAP), which was completed over 80 per cent in Sunamganj, 75 per cent in Habiganj and 71 per cent in Sylhet, a government official said. Dipak Ranjan Das, executive engineer, Bangladesh Water Development Board (BWDB), Sylhet, said some works on embankment and riverbank road could not be completed at the Sylhet-Assam frontiers in Zakiganj over the objection of India's Border Security Force. Stating that the project had been delayed for various reasons, Mr Das added that it is on the way towards completion within the new deadline. Sources in the government offices involved in the project said they are trying their best to complete the works within the updated deadline, which the FE understands that they intend to ensure completion within that deadline even if it slightly compromises quality. Infectious Diseases Probir Kumar Goshwami, additional chief engineer of north-east BWDB, said, "We would have to complete it in this fiscal as the progress is almost 80 per cent. It was taken after the greater Sylhet region and other haor districts suffered worst floods in 2022." The project is being implemented with significant financial support from the Asian Development Bank, while BWDB, Local Government Engineering Department, Department of Agricultural Extension (DAE) and Bangladesh Railway have also being assisting. For instance, one of the responsibilities of the DAE includes managing solar plant installations in the project area, while Bangladesh Railway would plant trees. After major irregularities were found during an investigation in the Sunamganj section of the project in 2025, BWDB officials were penalised and transferred. Some contractors had delayed works and among them Messrs Jamil Iqbal had left after the July Revolution. forsylhet@gmail.com Our Correspondent Published: Sep 29, 2026, 04:03 Share this news

Prev Next Officials say so far they’ve found just one mosquito infected with dengue fever in Pasco County and two cases involving people. By: Erik Waxler Posted 9:32 PM, Sep 24, 2026 Erik Waxler is committed to covering the stories that matter to you in the Greater Pasco County area. If you have a story idea, please email Erik@TampaBay28.com ODESSA, FL (WFTS) — With dengue fever cases mounting in neighboring Hillsborough County, Pasco County officials say they are not waiting for transmission of the mosquito-borne virus to become widespread locally. Pasco County has declared a local state of emergency and is encouraging other Tampa Bay area communities to do the same. Pasco County Fighting Off Dengue Fever Hillsborough County also declared a state of local emergency. The concern is on the mind of people like Patty McCloskey, who was heading back to her car after a hike at Starkey Wilderness Preserve. “I love the outdoors and nature and just being out in the fresh air,” McCloskey said. 1/1 Skip Ad Continue watchingafter the adVisit Advertiser websiteGO TO PAGE She said she was aware of the rising number of mosquito-borne dengue cases. She also discovered she had been bitten while outdoors. “It makes you not want to be out in nature, but sometimes you take that chance,” McCloskey said. Pasco County officials say they have found one mosquito infected with dengue and have confirmed two cases involving people. But with nearly 200 cases reported in neighboring Hillsborough County and one confirmed dengue-related death, Pasco officials say they are taking steps now to try to prevent a larger outbreak. The county's local state of emergency is expected to make it easier to get additional resources from the state. “They’ll be able to send additional resources, equipment, people to help with boots on the ground, chemicals that are needed to help combat the mosquitoes, within not just Pasco, but hopefully within our Tampa Bay region,” Pasco County Commissioner Seth Weightman said. Pasco County has been preparing for the threat of dengue for years. Tampa Bay 28 visited the Pasco County Mosquito Control District lab two years ago to see how staff members were working to protect residents from the virus. At the time, Executive Director Adriane Rogers explained how severe dengue can become. “Dengue is nicknamed breakbone fever. In more severe cases, we actually have issues where you feel like your bones are breaking. It’s that severe,” Rogers said. Now, mosquito control crews are collecting and testing mosquito samples and spraying insecticide in areas where mosquitoes could potentially spread the virus. Pasco is also lending one of its two mosquito control helicopters to Hillsborough County to assist with spraying there. Pasco officials say controlling the outbreak requires a regional response and are encouraging neighboring counties to take similar emergency action. “The issue in Hillsborough County is great. And the issue needs to be taken care of in Hillsborough County,” Pasco's Mosquito Control District Commissioner Michael Cox said. Residents can also help reduce the mosquito population around their homes. Officials recommend regularly checking yards for containers and other areas that collect standing water, where mosquitoes can breed. supplementary_news.content_title: Gene Networks Point to Interferon Decline as Driver of Severe Dengue in
supplementary_news.content: Dengue virus infects an estimated 390 million people each year, and roughly 96 million of them develop clinical or subclinical symptoms, a figure that is about three times higher than earlier World Health Organization estimates of the global burden. India carries a disproportionate share of that load, accounting for approximately 30 percent of infections worldwide, with many regions hyper-endemic and multiple viral serotypes co-circulating year-round. For most patients the illness resolves after a febrile phase, but a minority progress toward severe disease marked by thrombocytopenia, plasma leakage and, in the worst cases, shock. Predicting which patients will deteriorate remains one of the most pressing unsolved problems in dengue medicine, and a new study from New Delhi now offers a detailed molecular map of the earliest host responses that accompany the transition toward clinical severity. Writing in the journal New Microbes and New Infections, a team led by researchers at the CSIR Institute of Genomics and Integrative Biology and Max Hospital in New Delhi reports a whole-blood transcriptomic analysis of 112 dengue-positive patients recruited at their first hospital visit. The participants were classified according to the revised 2009 WHO guidelines into those without warning signs and those with warning signs, the latter defined by coagulation abnormalities such as thrombocytopenia, clinical fluid accumulation reflected in hemoconcentration, and increased vascular fragility. Within the group without warning signs, 46 patients also presented with leukopenia, allowing the investigators to stratify the cohort into mild, moderate and relatively severe subgroups. Although none of the patients met the formal criteria for severe dengue, the 21 patients carrying warning signs together with thrombocytopenia were treated as demonstrating a propensity for clinically severe outcomes because of their depressed platelet counts. The technical pipeline behind the study was considerable. The team isolated RNA from one milliliter of whole blood per patient, depleted globin and ribosomal RNA, and generated stranded sequencing libraries that were run as paired-end 151-base-pair reads on an Illumina NextSeq 2000 platform. The effort produced more than two billion reads, averaging about 18.5 million reads per sample. After quality trimming and quasi-mapping to the human transcriptome, differential expression was computed with DESeq2, and confounder analyses for age and sex showed no significant differences between the clinical groups. All 112 patients experienced primary dengue infection, and serotype analysis based on viral reads recovered from the sequencing data indicated that the majority were infected with DENV-2, consistent with the serotype circulating in Delhi during the study period. Samples were collected during the acute febrile phase, with a mean of 3.69 days of fever at enrollment. The clinical chemistry told a coherent story before any sequencing was considered. Total leukocyte counts, platelets, lymphocytes and neutrophils all differed significantly between the groups, with p-values below 0.001. The two leukopenic groups showed lower neutrophil and higher lymphocyte values than the mild group, a pattern the authors interpret as a subdued first-line defense, since neutrophils are the earliest active killers of pathogens during viral and bacterial infections. Notably, hematocrit was not elevated in the patients with warning signs, suggesting that capillary leak had not yet begun at the time of sampling. Liver function tests available for a subset of patients showed higher SGOT and SGPT values in the warning-sign group, along with significantly lower total protein and elevated bilirubin, although all values remained within normal ranges, hinting at hepatic derangement that was only beginning to emerge. Differential expression analysis between the moderate and mild groups yielded 15 significantly downregulated genes, most of them involved in immune response and inflammation, including the chemokine CXCL2, the neutrophil marker CD177, the acute-phase protein ORM1 and the inflammation regulator PI3. The authors read this as evidence of a subdued immune response in moderate patients compared with mild ones. By contrast, comparisons involving the severe group were far more dramatic: severe versus mild produced 215 upregulated and 92 downregulated genes, while severe versus moderate produced 142 upregulated and only 2 downregulated genes. Pathway enrichment against the Reactome database showed that upregulated functions in severe patients centered on glycosylation and the nervous system, whereas downregulated pathways encompassed immune and inflammatory response, GPCR signaling, platelet activation and aggregation, and prostaglandin synthesis in platelets and endothelial cells. One of the most intriguing findings was that, although many immune response genes were downregulated in severe patients, a diverse repertoire of B cell receptor genes, including immunoglobulin light and heavy chain variables, was upregulated, indicating an acute antibody response associated with severity. Upregulation of KIR3DL3, LILRB5 and IRAK1BP1 appeared to divert innate immune pathways toward resolution of inflammation. Taken together, the differential expression profile suggests an attenuation of immune and inflammatory activity in severe patients precisely at the time when platelet counts fall below normal thresholds due to platelet dysfunction, a counterintuitive pattern that complicates the traditional picture of dengue severity as a cytokine-driven hyperinflammatory state. To move beyond lists of individual genes, the team applied Weighted Gene Co-expression Network Analysis, or WGCNA, to 14,071 genes across all 112 samples. After selecting an optimal soft-threshold power to ensure scale-free network topology, the algorithm organized the genes into 22 modules, each representing a set of genes with highly similar expression patterns. The severe subgroup split into two major clades with starkly different co-expression patterns: clade 1 modules showed higher expression in severe patients and were enriched for metabolism, glycosylation, nervous system processes and DNA repair, while clade 2 modules showed decreased expression and carried functions related to blood coagulation, platelet activation, cell adhesion, immune response, regulation of virus replication, interferon response and cytokine signaling. Correlating module eigengenes with clinical parameters revealed that clade 2 modules correlated positively with platelet counts, while a single module, turquoise, correlated negatively, reinforcing the link between immune response modules and platelet dysregulation. Total leukocyte count, by contrast, showed no significant correlation with any module. Within the platelet-associated modules, the investigators identified a set of genes that collectively define the severe state. The greenyellow module contained interferon pathway genes such as IFI44L, IFI35, OAS1, SAMD9L and KAT2B, while the darkred module harbored genes governing platelet function, coagulation and endothelial integrity, including ARHGEF12, CTTN, SELP, PPBP, PRKAR2B and F13A1. Other modules captured vesicular trafficking genes such as GOLGA7 and RAB27B, thought to be required for viral replication and autophagy, and innate antiviral genes including IFIH1, which encodes the cytosolic RNA sensor MDA5, and HNRNPA2B1. When the team dichotomized the severe patients by platelet count, comparing those below 100 times 10 to the ninth per liter with those between 100 and 140, 16 genes showed significant differences in baseline transcript abundance, with IFI44L standing out at a difference of more than 800 counts per million. Regression analysis found no genes significantly correlated with SGOT, implying that modest transaminase elevations do not substantially shape disease outcome. The findings converge with transcriptomic studies of dengue patients in Brazil, where interferon-stimulated genes such as IFI27 and ISG15 emerged as biomarkers capable of distinguishing dengue hemorrhagic fever from uncomplicated dengue during the late acute phase. Although IFI27 was not captured in the Indian dataset, ISG15 was consistently upregulated in patients with warning signs and low platelets, aligning with its proposed role as a severity marker. The Indian study also detected CTTN, a gene tied to endothelial barrier function that was not a focus of the Brazilian datasets, hinting at population-specific elements of the immune-endothelial axis. The authors propose a sequential pathogenic cascade for patients with warning signs: a suboptimal early interferon and innate immune response weakens host defenses and permits viral replication, heightened viral stress drives platelet dysfunction and clearance, and, independently of cytokine-mediated hyperinflammation, upregulation of O-linked glycosylation genes such as GALNT13, B4GALT1 and B3GNT4 alongside downregulation of structural genes like CTTN alters the endothelial glycocalyx, producing the vascular permeability that characterizes the onset of clinical warning signs. The study carries the inherent limitation of a cross-sectional design, since blood was drawn at a single acute-phase time point, and whole-blood RNA means the observed signatures may partly reflect shifts in circulating cell composition rather than purely transcriptional changes within individual cell types. The authors note that single-cell transcriptomics or computational deconvolution in future longitudinal cohorts would help resolve cell-type-specific contributions. Even so, the work suggests practical avenues: monitoring glycocalyx-related gene signatures could enable early identification of patients at risk of severe disease, and therapeutic strategies aimed at preserving glycocalyx integrity may offer a novel way to reduce vascular complications. If validated across larger and more geographically diverse cohorts, the interferon and glycosylation signatures identified here could become molecular biomarkers for predicting, and perhaps mitigating, severe dengue before the first warning signs appear. Daily Excelsior 03:11 PM Sep 28, 2026 IST Bhaderwah/Jammu, Sep 28: Doda has reported a spike in dengue cases, with 52 patients admitted to hospitals, prompting civic authorities to intensify anti-larval spraying, fogging and public awareness campaigns, officials said on Monday. As part of the special drive, civic teams of the Doda and Bhaderwah Municipal Committees have conducted door-to-door inspections in several areas over the past three days to identify and eliminate mosquito breeding sites, officials said. They said 52 people have been admitted to the Government Medical College Hospital in Doda. Advertisement Executive Officer of the Doda and Bhaderwah Municipal Committees, Ravi Saini, said six teams, three each in Doda and Bhaderwah, have been deployed for fogging and anti-larval spraying in vulnerable areas and locations from where a higher number of dengue cases have been reported. "We have intensified anti-dengue measures in both municipalities and, till Monday morning, identified and destroyed nearly 239 mosquito breeding spots on residential, religious and commercial premises," Saini said. The anti-dengue drive will continue until the outbreak is brought under control, he said. Authorities have warned residents and commercial establishments where mosquito breeding sites are repeatedly found, saying they could face penalties if such sites are detected again. Health Inspector of the National Vector Borne Diseases Control Programme (NVBDCP), Liaqat Ali Zargar, said 52 people with severe dengue infection were admitted to GMC Doda in the past seven days. "The number may have risen today as fresh data will be issued only after samples of 90 people suspected to be infected with dengue undergo NS1 ELISA testing," Zargar said. Health authorities have issued an advisory urging citizens to take preventive measures amid rising infections. Authorities have advised senior citizens and people who have diabetes, hypertension, respiratory illnesses and other comorbidities to remain vigilant and seek medical attention if they develop symptoms or their condition worsens. LogOut HOMEPAGE U.S. News Florida Counties Declare State of Emergency Over Dengue Fever Outbreak DEADLY VIRUS One death has been confirmed in the Sunshine State this year. Reagin von Lehe Breaking News Intern Updated Sep. 29 2026 6:58AM EDT / Published Sep. 28 2026 4:42PM EDT Comments Joe Raedle/Getty Images Health officials in several Tampa Bay counties have declared a local state of emergency over the past few days due to a major dengue fever outbreak. The mosquito-borne viral illness, notorious for intense joint pain, is often called “breakbone fever.” Dengue is more common in tropical countries but has been increasing in the U.S. in recent years. The Florida Department of Health has reported 190 cases so far this year—Florida’s second-highest total on record, behind the 199 cases in 2023. By comparison, the state recorded 62 cases last year. The last major U.S. outbreak outside the Texas-Mexico border occurred in 2009. Residents of Pinellas, Pasco and Hillsborough counties have been urged to dump standing water from garbage cans, gutters and buckets, maintain chlorinated pools, and report mosquito problems. Most U.S. cases are linked to travel to the Caribbean, Central and South America, Southeast Asia, and Pacific islands. “This is wildly unusual for us,” a Hillsborough County spokesperson told ABC News. Experts point to warm temperatures, heavy rain, and Florida’s proximity to Puerto Rico as conditions that have helped mosquitoes multiply. One death—an elderly woman—has been confirmed. Credit : Getty NEED TO KNOW Clearwater, Fla., released 10,000 mosquitofish to control mosquito populations amid rising cases of dengue fever The prevalence of the disease, transmitted by mosquito bites, has prompted local states of emergency in several Tampa Bay counties Mosquitofish naturally eat mosquito larvae and are a sustainable, environmentally friendly solution in the U.S. to combat the disease threat A city in Florida is working to combat the rising cases of dengue fever. On Friday, Sept. 25, the city of Clearwater, Florida, released about 10,000 eastern mosquitofish — known for their appetite for mosquito larvae — into four bodies of water in hopes of curbing the mosquito population, per WFLA. The move is part of the city’s effort to reduce the possibility of residents contracting dengue fever. According to Mayo Clinic, dengue fever is a disease that is transmitted through mosquito bites in “tropical and subtropical” regions of the world. While it has been historically most common in Southeast Asia, the western Pacific Islands, Africa and Latin America, dengue fever has also since appeared in the United States and Europe. A house mosquito. Getty The illness can present flu-like symptoms, including a high fever, while a more serious version of the disease can result in bleeding, a sudden blood pressure drop or, possibly, death. Efforts to curb disease contraction center on avoiding mosquito bites and reducing mosquito populations. The frequency of the disease has risen so significantly in recent months that several Tampa Bay counties, including Hillsborough, Pasco and Pinellas, have declared local states of emergency. Enter mosquitofish, a fish in the guppy family that naturally feeds on mosquito larvae, making them an effective and environmentally conscious way to decrease the prevalence of mosquitoes, per Santa Clara County (which uses the fish for mosquito control). Mosquitofish (gambusia). Getty Mosquitofish, also known as gambusia, can become invasive, since they are native to parts of North and Central America, that’s not a concern in the United States. So it’s a long-standing, sustainable way to reduce the mosquito population.” Per the outlet, Clearwater has ordered another 31,000 mosquitofish to be released in the city. Photograph: Smith Collection/Gado/Getty Images Dengue fever outbreak prompts Florida counties to declare state of emergency CDC says 392 cases of Dengue were reported for the year so far in the state, along with different county-level data Several Florida counties recently declared a state of local emergency in response to a spate of dengue fever infections. Hillsborough county, Florida, officials made the declaration on 24 September as health authorities recorded 134 confirmed cases of dengue fever, which is a mosquito-borne sickness typically found in countries outside the US. Officials said that the spread of the illness poses “an immediate and widespread threat to the public health, safety, and welfare of the residents and visitors of Hillsborough county”. Controlling the tropical disease – often referred to as breakbone fever because it can cause extreme pain – requires “immediate, aggressive, and continuous” measures such as pesticide application, public education and emergency resource planning, officials said. Dengue cases have become more common in parts of the US. In 2023, Long Beach and Pasadena reported the first ever known locally acquired cases in California. The spread of dengue mosquitoes outside tropical and subtropical locales has even hit England, with authorities recently announcing that Aedes aegypti had been found in east London homes. Scientists have said that global warming is poised to intensify climate-related diseases. Declaring a local state of emergency enables Hillsborough county – whose seat is the city of Tampa – to request “any available and necessary state, federal, and local emergency funds, grants, financial assistance, and mutual aid” in their ongoing fight against mosquitoes carrying dengue. The initial declaration was put into effect for one week, but officials can extend it. Neighboring Pasco and Pinellas counties have also declared similar states of emergency in relation to dengue reports. The Florida department of health said in its recent report on mosquito-transmitted viruses that there were 26 cases of international travel-linked dengue reported in the state during a six-day period beginning on 13 September. As of Monday, the CDC noted 392 cases of dengue had been reported overall in Florida for the year so far, along with different county-level data. Symptoms show up between three days and two weeks after a bite from an infected mosquito. Among the symptoms are “sudden onset of fever, severe headache, eye pain, muscle and joint pain ... and bleeding. Gastrointestinal symptoms like vomiting and diarrhea may also be present in some cases,” Florida’s state health department said. The symptoms typically span four days to one week. supplementary_news.content: Health Child Dengue Surges as Siem Reap Hospital Runs Out of Beds The hospital has only 1,129 beds, so many patients are being treated on the floor. Nurses work in rotation to care for them. Chantana said the staff is experienced in treating dengue but this year's caseload is unusually heavy. Photo: Iv Phanith By: Isa Rohany and Iv Phanith September 30, 2026 , 11:50 AM 00:00 / 01:35 SIEM REAP – The Jayavarman VII Children's Hospital in Siem Reap is treating a sharp rise in dengue fever this year. Over 38 weeks, 14,101 children have been treated for the disease, and doctors say 10 to 15 percent developed severe dengue. Some 1,964 people are now at the hospital, also known as Kantha Bopha III. These include 1,653 children and 311 pregnant women, director Yay Chantana said. “On a single day, the hospital admitted 115 dengue patients, 42 with dengue accompanied by bleeding, and 31 with shock or other severe forms of the disease,” he said. The hospital has only 1,129 beds, so many patients are being treated on the floor. Nurses work in rotation to care for them. Chantana said the staff is experienced in treating dengue but this year's caseload is unusually heavy. Severe dengue can cause a dangerous loss of plasma and blood. Without timely hospital treatment to replace those fluids, children can die. Chantana attributes the rise partly to climate change and the El Nino weather pattern, which they say speeds up mosquitoes' metabolism. The mosquitoes bite more often, and the disease can spread quickly from child to child, sometimes within about five days. Dengue is seasonal, peaking in July, August and September. He hopes October will bring fewer cases. Cases by province Siem Reap has recorded about 5,000 cases this year, followed by Kampong Thom and Banteay Meanchey with about 2,500 each. Battambang has recorded 1,700 cases, with these being the most severe among the provinces. Hospital doctors have trained medical staff in Siem Reap, Battambang, Oddar Meanchey, Banteay Meanchey, Pailin, Pursat, Preah Vihear and Kampong Thom provinces. Training teams travel to local sites because many people buy medicine over the counter. Taking too much can damage the liver and kidneys and make dengue worse, Chantana said. Some parents, unaware of the risks, also take their children for intravenous fluids on their own. Too much can worsen the illness. There is no specific medicine or vaccine for dengue. Treatment consists of managing high fever and, when patients lose plasma, giving fluids under a doctor's supervision. Parents should seek emergency care immediately if a child vomits or there is blood in vomit, urine or stool, which are signs of severe dengue. He advised not to buy drugs without a prescription. Philstar.com hosts its content but has no editorial control over it. September 30, 2026 | 12:00am A gym at the National Kidney and Transplant Institute in Quezon City became a leptospirosis ward as cases ballooned due to flooding from Typhoon Carina in this file photo from August 2024. Miguel De Guzman ADVERTISEMENT MANILA, Philippines — The number of leptospirosis cases in the country is increasing, with nearly 12,000 infections recorded this year, while dengue numbers have dropped, according to the Department of Health. As of Sept. 23, DOH data showed 11,965 leptospirosis cases have been reported, which is 46 percent higher than 8,189 cases in the same period last year. From Aug. 27 to Sept. 9, however, the DOH monitored a decline in the number of cases after 3,284 infections were recorded, compared to 3,330 cases from Aug. 6 to 19. Despite possible reporting delays, the one percent decrease may signal that the current surge is easing, the DOH said. The cumulative case fatality rate stands at 5.08 percent, lower than last year’s 10.53-percent CFR. People should seek medical advice upon exposure to floods, with or without symptoms, the DOH stressed. Cumulative dengue cases this year remains lower at 168,060 cases, a 30 percent drop compared to 239,001 cases during the same period last year. The DOH recorded an eight percent increase in the recent three to four weeks with 21,122 cases, compared to the previous five to six weeks with 19,572 cases. Up to 656 deaths were reported, which is 28 percent lower than last year’s 910. Forty-eight percent, or 312, of fatalities were clinically classified as severe dengue. Students were identified as the most affected population. Zero-balance billing Close to 50 public hospitals benefited from the P1 billion released for the implementation of the zero-balance billing program, the DOH said. The budget will be spread out in 48 hospitals in Aklan, Batangas, Benguet, Laguna, Quezon and Sarangani. Fifteen Laguna hospitals were allocated P294.1 million, while 12 hospitals in Batangas were provided P141.1 million. In Quezon, 11 hospitals were allotted P152.85 million. Four hospitals in Benguet were allocated P114.99 million, four in Sarangani will receive P84.2 million and two in Aklan will have P212.69 million. Under the program, no payment is required from patients for hospital services, including medical procedures, doctor’s professional fees and medications. Daily Excelsior 04:43 AM Sep 29, 2026 IST Excelsior Correspondent DODA, Sept 28: Cases of dengue have increased in the mountainous district Doda with the concerned authorities claiming 58 reported cases so far. Executive Officer (EO) of Municipal Committee Doda and Bhaderwah, Ravi Saini informed that as dengue cases continue to rise, they ramped up intensive anti-larval spraying, fogging operations at markets, public conveniences, mosques and house-to-house inspections to curb mosquito breeding. Advertisement “Six teams have been formed with three each for Bhaderwah and Doda towns to carry out the fogging and anti-larval sprays in the vulnerable areas from where maximum cases were reported,” he said adding that they have so far identified and destroyed about 239 mosquito breeding spots at residential, religious and commercial premises. “Last year such cases stood at 70,” Chief Medical Officer (CMO) Doda, Dr. Vinod Sharma informed adding that personnel from the municipality were carrying out fogging operation and clearing stagnant water on war footing to control the spread of dengue. He also informed that municipal workers were visiting door-to-door to educate the people on preventive measures. The concerned authorities have warned residents and commercial establishments that penalties can be imposed if breeding sites are detected in their premises. Health Inspector National Vector Borne Diseases Control Programme, Liaqat Ali Zargar informed that during last seven days, 50 persons with severe dengue infection were admitted in GMC Doda. Meanwhile, the health authorities have issued advisory urging citizens to take preventive measures and contact the doctor in case of fever, cough, sore throat or breathing difficulties. supplementary_news.content_title: Pasco County dengue cases rise to 3 amid declared state of emergency
supplementary_news.content: The Brief Pasco County officials declared a local state of emergency after health officials confirmed three locally acquired dengue fever cases. The emergency declaration gives county administrators expanded authority for seven days to waive everyday procedures and coordinate mosquito control efforts. Medical experts warn that dengue causes severe joint and muscle pain, with critical warning signs typically appearing as fever subsides. PASCO COUNTY, Fla. - Following a declared a state of emergency in Pasco County, health officials confirmed three locally contracted cases of dengue fever Friday. Pasco County emergency response What we know Pasco County issued a seven-day emergency declaration on Wednesday following two confirmed locally transmitted dengue fever cases reported by the Florida Department of Health in Pasco County. Since yesterday, that number has risen to three. The designation gives the county administrator and emergency management director immediate authority to waive everyday operational procedures to safeguard public safety while assisting local mosquito control crews. Protecting home and family What you can do Health officials strongly urge residents to protect themselves using "Drain and Cover" principles to eliminate mosquito breeding environments. Residents should dump out standing water, wear light-colored long-sleeved clothing with closed-toed shoes outside, and apply CDC-recommended insect repellents containing DEET, Picaridin, IR3535, or Oil of Lemon Eucalyptus. Symptoms and warning signs What they're saying Medical professionals warn that dengue virus causes excruciating pain, earning it the moniker "break-bone fever". "The body aches are so intense that it's got this nickname as 'break-bone fever,'" said Dr. Kartik Cherabuddi, chief hospital epidemiology officer at Tampa General Hospital. "It's real, and I've seen patients — they hurt so bad, it's the predominant thing that’s bringing them into the emergency room". Disease progression details By the numbers Only about 25% of people bitten by an infected mosquito develop symptoms, meaning 75% remain asymptomatic. However, asymptomatic individuals can still pass the virus to other mosquitoes that bite them, which can then spread infection to other people. High-risk groups and ER visits Why you should care Roughly one in 20 symptomatic patients develops severe complications, with symptoms usually appearing two weeks after a mosquito bite. High-risk groups include infants, pregnant women, adults 65 and older, immunocompromised individuals, and anyone previously infected with dengue. Cherabuddi warned that critical warning signs often emerge right when fever drops. "The next two days is when you can have more severe warning signs," Cherabuddi said. "If you have severe abdominal pain, persistently throwing up, bleeding from the gums or other sites, difficulty breathing — and critically, that’s when the fever starts to go down is when these could develop. That's when you absolutely have to go to the ER". The Source The information in this story was gathered from the Pasco Board of County Commissioners, who announced the emergency declaration, as well as Florida Department of Health data and statements from Tampa General Hospital

supplementary_news.content_title: Dengue: Recovery doesn’t end at hospital discharge
supplementary_news.content: Health Dengue: Recovery doesn’t end at hospital discharge Exhaustion lingering long after discharge is clinically recognised as post-dengue fatigue syndrome When 32-year-old Diya, a software professional from Kochi, was discharged from the hospital after a gruelling six-day bout with dengue fever, she assumed the hardest part was over. Her fever had vanished, her blood pressure had stabilised, and her platelet counts had safely crossed normal thresholds. Hospital staff handed her a discharge summary stamped “cured,” but a week later, when Diya logged back into her desk job, she realised her battle with dengue had merely entered its second phase. Sitting at her computer, Diya was overwhelmed by physical and mental exhaustion. Simple tasks left her trembling with fatigue, and climbing a short flight of stairs forced her to pause halfway to catch her breath. Weeks later, another wave of distress arrived: large strands of hair began coming loose during daily brushing. On paper, Diya was a healthy dengue survivor; in reality, she was living through the frustrating “long tail” of post-dengue recovery. Her experience reflects a widespread yet frequently overlooked phenomenon following seasonal dengue outbreaks. While public health messaging naturally focuses on managing the acute phase — tracking fever spikes and preventing plasma leakage — the weeks following clearance present their own silent struggle. The return of normal blood parameters does not instantly translate to functional fitness or cellular recovery. The exhaustion lingering long after discharge is clinically recognised as post-dengue fatigue syndrome. Dr Vinod Xavier, consultant in internal medicine at Aster Medcity in Kochi, notes that fatigue can persist for several weeks after the virus clears. This weakness stems from severe inflammation, physical deconditioning from bed rest, reduced nutritional intake, and general physiological stress. Most patients gradually improve with structured nutrition, hydration, and rest, though persistent or worsening symptoms warrant further clinical evaluation. For working adults and students, this physical drag creates significant friction. Employers and families often expect an immediate bounce-back once fever resolves. However, inside the body, the immune system is actively clearing metabolic debris and repairing tissue damage. Pushing through this weakness through sheer willpower frequently backfires, delaying recovery. This recovery curve is equally crucial for paediatric patients returning to school and sports. Parents often worry when a child cleared of active infection continues to lack energy. “Once the critical phase of dengue passes, serious complications are unlikely,” notes Dr Sheeja Sugunan, associate professor and paediatric intensivist at SAT Hospital, Government Medical College, Thiruvananthapuram. “However, tiredness and weakness can last for many days, especially if the child had a severe infection.” Dr Sheeja emphasises that because every child recovers differently, there is no fixed timeline for regaining strength. “Parents can send their child back to school as soon as the child feels well enough. However, it is important to make sure they get plenty of rest, drink enough fluids, and eat well while their body fully recovers,” she adds. Adding to post-viral distress is sudden, dramatic hair shedding weeks after recovery. Edwina Raj, head of services in clinical nutrition and dietetics at Aster CMI Hospital in Bengaluru, points out that hair fall typically presents weeks to months after the illness. High fever, sharp drops in food intake, and rapid weight loss act as a shock to the system, causing active hair follicles to prematurely shift into a resting state known as telogen effluvium. While this delayed shedding triggers anxiety, Edwina stresses it is a temporary stress response rather than permanent damage. The priority during this phase is overall metabolic support through adequate protein, balanced calories, hydration, and sleep, while strictly avoiding crash diets or mega-dosing supplements, which add strain to a recovering system. Rebuilding depleted reserves requires a gentle, steady dietary approach. Recovery diets should prioritise protein alongside iron, zinc, B-complex vitamins, and vitamin D through simple foods like lentils, eggs, curd, nuts, seeds, and leafy greens. To restore gut health without causing digestive distress, meals should be reintroduced gradually in small portions alongside fermented foods like curd. Protecting the liver, which often suffers transient inflammation during dengue, is equally critical. Rather than restrictive ‘detox’ diets or herbal cleanses, the liver recovers best when spared from alcohol, heavily processed foods, excess refined sugars, and fried items. Recovery is not an instant event marked by a lab report, but a quiet process unfolding over weeks. By respecting post-viral fatigue, allowing time for tissue reset, and prioritising proper nourishment, both adult and paediatric patients can safely navigate the long tail of dengue to regain full vitality. The Florida Department of Health reported at least 190 cases of locally acquired dengue fever in the state this year, with 170 of those cases in Hillsborough County alone. Advertisement Lee County Mosquito Control said it is monitoring activity in the area.
